Madam Speaker, this bill amends the Competition Act as it pertains to the advertising of the price of goods.
When goods are advertised for a certain price and someone goes into the store to buy them, they do not know what they will have to pay because invariably there is at least the GST on it, there may be a PST on it, there may be a tire tax on it and there may be another charge on it of some kind. The charges go on and on and a person has no idea what they have to pay for the goods.
This bill requires merchants to declare the dollar value of every tax or charge on every item sold in the marketplace unless the item is declared to include all taxes and charges. In other words, if you want to sell you specify the taxes all the way down the line in dollar amounts or you sell tax included.

speechtext: The Chair would want to hold that nobody would be impugning motives to anybody else and that members would be careful in not giving the impression that they are impugning motives.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I certainly would not wish to do that, but I do believe I am entitled to my opinion that what constitutes a waste of time is nevertheless a waste of time. I would submit that quite possibly there are many Canadians who would agree with me that our job here is to get on with governing the nation and not to debate the same thing twice.
I would suggest that people who disagree with this bill or any other bill brought forward by this government should simply speak and vote against it rather than force extra stages in the debate that are of no productive consequence whatsoever.
Speaking to the bill, which is what I intend to do, the specifics of this legislation will ensure the government can meet additional borrowing requirements of $8.2 billion over those granted by this House in April of last year.
The reason for these increased requirements is no mystery. The slow pace of economic recovery in Canada, the result of a global recession, has combined with lower than expected inflation to significantly reduce government revenues from what we had forecast. At the same time our spending obligations under unemployment insurance and transfer programs to the provinces have been pushed higher due to the same economic weaknesses.
I will expand on the details of the bill in a few moments, but first I want to address the broader issue of government borrowing and the vital importance of deficit and debt control.
Deficit and debt control are not subjects of great interest to my hon. friends opposite just in some of the suggestions put forward a few minutes ago. We continually hear suggestions from the other side as to how the government can spend more money.
At the same time we hear the Leader of the Opposition in an absolutely remarkable statement suggesting that he is going to eliminate the GST. He has absolutely no idea whatsoever where he is going to get the $15 billion to $17 billion in revenue that it accrues, unless of course it is through this hidden tax on everything
Government Orders
including food and medical services that we understand is being considered. However, that is for next year because they can only come up with one idea a year it seems.
Meanwhile our hon. friends in the New Democratic Party seem to have no sense whatsoever of the concept of controlling expenditures. I sat here in the House the other day when the leader of the New Democratic Party got up and proposed that the way the government could accrue a whole lot more revenue was to eliminate expenses being claimed by businesses for things like lunches and dinners and hospitality which has been a long-standing practice in this country. Maybe my hon. friend is right, maybe those things should be eliminated. I might say I was rather amazed last night when I attended a reception hosted by the Canadian Food and Restaurant Association. I noticed virtually every member of the New Democratic caucus there, including the leader, enjoying themselves to the fullest.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: They were at the trough.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Right there just having the most enjoyable time. I wonder what that says about the seriousness of those intentions.
The point I am making is that this government takes very seriously the idea of debt and deficit control. That is why this government has brought forward tough measures. These have made this government very unpopular at times because everybody likes to have services but nobody really wants to pay the taxes which pay for them.
Our predecessors found a solution to the problem. They did not pay for them. They let the debt and deficit simply grow. In fact, if the measures brought in by this government had not been put in place, this country's deficit would be approaching $100 billion today. That would be totally unacceptable by those of us on this side. I know that they have voted against every cost control measure brought in by this government during the four years plus that I have had the privilege of being here.
It is important for people to understand as we bring forward this legislation that there are different philosophies in this House. The guiding philosophy of our party is that painful as it sometimes is, you have to pay your way as you go. Really in the final analysis the idea that governments should spend and spend and spend and let their grandchildren pay the bill is simply not one that is acceptable to us.

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
In his statement, my hon. colleague, the Minister of Finance, powerfully summarized why this concern is so justified. He pointed out and I quote from his remarks of that day:
"Excessive government deficits, both federal and provincial, have contributed to a level of net foreign debt far higher for Canada than for any other G-7 country. This large net foreign debt, public sector and private, means that Canadians paid more than $22 billion in net interest last year to foreign lenders. That is money that Canadians cannot use to develop our economy. This adds up to the economic damage done by the higher interest rates and higher taxes that resulted from higher government deficits".
Harsh foreign indebtedness. Severe restraints on government's ability to assist people and build economic strength. Higher interest rates and higher taxes. These make up the painful price Canadians are paying today because previous governments put deficit and debt control on the back burner or ignored it altogether.
That is why since coming into office the keystone of this government's policies has been spending restraint and deficit reduction. This has meant taking firm and sometimes unpopular actions and decisions, such as closing military bases, privatizing organizations as the post office has been doing, reducing the number of employees on the federal payroll and putting limits on the growth of some provincial transfers. Now that is not to say that governments cannot learn to be more sensitive sometimes in the way these things are done.
It is extremely important, for example, as Canada Post carries out its conversion process that there be full and adequate consultation with the people in the communities. A moment ago I heard an hon. friend opposite present a petition with respect to an impending closure in his area. As a rural member I can say it is a cause of great anxiety in small rural communities when the big machine comes in and says: "Guess what? Your postmaster or postmistress is retiring and your post office is gone". It is important for Canada Post to be sensitive to those communities, to listen to what the people have to say and to provide them with the reasonable assurances they are looking for that in actual fact they are going to be provided with the same quality of service under the new approach as under the old. That is the key thing.
The same thing is true with respect to base closures. We have an overcapacity of military bases by some 40 per cent to 50 per cent. We cannot ask the Department of National Defence to use up its budget completely by maintaining antiquated equipment or infrastructure. However, the government has to do some planning. If there is going to be a base phased out the government must know what ameliorative measures or plans it is going to put in place so as not to devastate the economy and social life of the community.
That is critically important in rural areas like southwestern Nova Scotia where there is tremendous concern today about the future of CFB Cornwallis. I was very pleased to see the new Minister of National Defence recognize this point shortly after she took on that important responsibility. I want to say to her and to the House that there are many people throughout southwestern Nova Scotia concerned about the future of Cornwallis. I look forward to some early indication from the Minister of National Defence and the government with respect to what the plans are for Cornwallis in the short and long term.
As I was saying before, the actions the government has undertaken have been difficult but they have produced results. Last year's deficit was still significantly lower as a share of our economy than that in 1984-85. That is even despite the impact of the recession. Between 1984 and 1990 we had the lowest real program spending growth of any of the G-7 countries. I might also say that it was significantly below the growth levels of any of the provinces in this country. Most important, we have achieved a major turnaround in the basic structure of government spending.
When this government came into office in 1984 it was the beneficiary of a $16.1 billion operating deficit that was a legacy of the predecessor government. It was paying another $22.5 billion in interest costs on the national debt for a total deficit of $38.5 billion.
As I mentioned before, had there been no change in the course, today that deficit would have just naturally grown. Following along with the inertia that had developed over those years it would have been dose to $100 billion. This is totally, totally unacceptable. We would now be approaching the point where the World Bank would be saying: "We are taking over".
February 4, 1993

It is really an issue of sovereignty in the final analysis. The difficult measures this government has taken on in tackling the deficit problem is a defence of Canadian sovereignty.
At that time the government was spending $1.33 for every dollar of taxes it took in. Imagine how a household would do when a pay cheque of $500 is brought home every two weeks but $700 is spent. Boy, where would that leave you in the long term? That is what the previous government was doing.
In 1987-88 however we eliminated the operating deficit and transformed it into a surplus to the point that today the government is operating in the black to the tune of $6.6 billion a year.
We hear a lot of talk about deficits and about the amount of the deficit but it is important to understand and to recall the structure of that deficit and the structure of the debt. Our friends left not only a $16.1 billion operating deficit, but also a debt of over $200 billion.
While this government has been working to bring the operating deficit down to the point where it crossed the line and is now operating a surplus, the interest has still been accumulating on that $227 billion debt that was the legacy of the Trudeau government to the children of future generations of Canadians. If the interest that has accrued on that debt is combined, it is up to something in the order of $450 billion. This government has been operating in the black for the last four years. In fact we have been able to control the growth of that national debt to the point that it is more than $30 billion less than it would have been otherwise.
This is complicated stuff. Sometimes it is even difficult for members on the other side to understand, but it is not very hard for any Canadian to understand that if we annually spend more money than we are taking in then we will get ourselves into serious trouble. We can all understand and relate to that.
That is precisely what the Trudeau government was doing for years and that is precisely what has burdened Canadians not only for this generation and for the next generation but for our grandchildren. That is what it has come down to.
If the programs and the approach to deficit control that have been put in place by this government stay in
Government Orders
place, as they will after this government is returned for its third mandate some time during the course of this year, we will eventually get out of that cycle and Canadians will live with money in the bank in future generations as they should. A country with the wealth and resources of this country has no excuse for having to operate in the red at all.
Meanwhile we still have to pay interest payments on Mr. Trudeau's debt. That means further deficits, still growing debt and the interest charges that the debt imposes. We face the added challenges of pursuing fiscal responsibility at a time of slow economic recovery when Canadians are looking to government to do what it can to bolster new growth and job creation. This means we need to do more to break that vicious deficit-debt cycle and also to free up resources for new government investment in Canada's economic growth and competitiveness.
As the Minister of Finance announced last December we are pursuing those investments. We are taking concrete action to aid small business, to improve R and D incentives, to lever better working training and to expand national investment in infrastructure.
To fund these investments while restraining this year's deficit and bringing it down more sharply next year we must reduce government spending in other areas. This too is being done. Let me remind this House and all Canadians of some of the actions announced in December's economic and fiscal statement. These are spending control measures that will contribute to savings of nearly $8 billion over the balance of this fiscal year and the next two.
Let me list a few. For two years salaries will be frozen for public servants and employees of non-commercial Crown corporations. A similar regime will be applied to commercial Crown corporations that depend on federal funding. This does not mean that our public servants do not deserve increases and it does not mean that they do not need increases. However the reality is that we have to pay from within the resources that are available. I suspect that we have the best quality public servants of any country in the world. They are dedicated people who serve Canadians. The reality is that we must cut the cloth according to the pattern.

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
Salaries will also be frozen for two years for the Governor General, Lieutenant Governors, the Prime Minister, cabinet ministers, members of Parliament, senators and the federal judiciary. Everybody is involved in this.
Operating budgets of government departments will be cut by 3 per cent. They are not getting an increase in their budgets. They are decreasing by 3 per cent. Including the wage freeze federal operating budgets will be 5 per cent lower than planned levels in each of the next two fiscal years. They are going to have to work hard to to do the jobs they must do with fewer resources available to do them.
The UI benefit rate will be reduced from 60 per cent to 57 per cent to ensure a freeze in the average benefit that is received. Nobody will get less money than they are getting now but there will be a freeze.
Grants and subsidies to most organizations and interest groups will be cut by 10 per cent in each of the next two years.
These actions will bring the estimated deficit down to $34.4 billion this year and $32.6 billion next year, compared to our budget forecast of $27.5 billion for 1992-93 and $22.5 billion for 1993-94. That is a result of the impact of lost revenues.
This slippage will totally be the result of the weaker than anticipated economy on revenues. With the action we are taking program spending over the next two fiscal years will be similar to that projected in the February 1992 budget. The government is not spending any more. This undesired and certainly unwelcome increase in the deficit is not a result of this government spending more nor is it a result of the dollar being out of whack because of the spending guidelines set down by the minister a year ago. It is a result of the revenue side being down. That is what has really put things out of whack and created a higher deficit. This is a result of weaker than anticipated revenues.
Again let me remind the House of what the minister said last year. He said:
The expenditure reductions announced in this statement provide a considerable reduction in the structural component of the deficit. As such, the deficit should decline rapidly through the medium term on the basis of the tight control over spending in place, stronger economic performance and lower interest rates. It remains the
government's objective to attain zero financial requirements over
the medium term.
Let me turn to the main provision of the supplementary borrowing authority bill. First, the amount of the supplementary borrowing authority being requested is based on currently estimated financial requirements of $30.5 billion for the year, up $10.8 billion from the February budget. This reflects the impact of the economy on revenues. There is an additional $1.8 billion requirement for loans to the CDIC but at the same time our total requirements have been partially offset by $4.4 billion relating to foreign exchange operations. As a result, the final net additional borrowing requirement is $8.2 billion.
Let me provide some additional information on the $1.8 billion that the CDIC will likely borrow from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. This reflects the financial difficulties experienced in recent years by two member institutions.
Some $500 million represents what CDIC paid out to cover insured deposits held at Shoppers Trust when it was liquidated last year. The remainder has been used for loans in respect of Central Guaranty Trust. This is to help fund the acquisition of certain Central Guaranty assets and all deposit liabilities by the Toronto Dominion Bank. The loan for Central Guaranty covers the shortfall between assumed liabilities and assets and is secured by the remaining assets of the firm.
Let me briefly review the impact of foreign exchange operations. These have worked in two directions. On the negative side there has been a requirement of $1 billion to cover gains in foreign currencies held in the exchange fund account and another $3 billion to replenish foreign exchange reserves. However, these additions have been more than offset by $8.4 billion in intervention operations. This has resulted in a positive balance that has reduced borrowing requirements by $4.4 billion. Therefore the final net need is $8.3 billion.
I should also explain that this bill contains two concluding clauses dealing with unused borrowing authority that was previously granted by this House.
Clause 3 ensures that all unused borrowing authority in excess of $3 billion granted under this legislation will be cancelled on March 31,1993. This is a standard clause and allows a non-lapsing $3 billion contingency reserve to be carried forward into the next fiscal year.
February 4, 1993

Clause 4, the concluding clause, ensures that all unused borrowing authority granted under legislation earlier this year will also be cancelled on March 31, 1993. This provision makes certain that only the one non-lapsing reserve for $3 billion can be carried forward into next year.
I firmly believe that the government's expenditure control measures, those we have taken in the past as well as those announced in December, offer solid evidence that we are continuing to handle the nation's finances prudently and well.
It is also important to remember where so much of the government spending supported by this bill actually goes. Transfer payments to individuals, including unemployment insurance and old age security, represent the single greatest share of government program spending. These are followed by transfers to provinces, which include support for social welfare programs and education.
This is spending that plays an important part in helping disadvantaged Canadians deal with the difficulties imposed by slow recovery and widespread industrial restructuring. This bill will ensure that the government can meet its obligations while remaining committed to the action needed to bring Canada's fiscal situation back in balance over the medium term.
I apologize to the translators for speaking so quickly at times, thank the House for its indulgence and commend the bill to all members.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to respond on behalf of the Official Opposition to the speech by the parliamentary secretary moving third reading of this bill.
In commending this bill to the House the hon. member attempted to blame the high level of borrowing authority sought in that bill on the weak government revenues which he said came about because of the weak economy. In this case, he has said something with which the House can be in agreement.
The weak economy has not only devastated the lives of more than 1.6 million Canadians who are out of work, it has not only devastated the lives of thousands of small business people who have been forced into unwanted bankruptcy, it has not only caused the loss of billions of dollars of production, but also all of this has meant
Government Orders
weaker government revenues. People who are out of work do not pay taxes. Businesses going into bankruptcy do not pay taxes.
In trying to excuse the weaker than anticipated government revenues, to find an excuse for these revenues because of the weak economy, my hon. friend reminds me of the individual who was brought before the court accused of murdering his parents and then pleaded for mercy on the grounds he was an orphan.
This economy is weak and government revenues are weak because of the deliberate action of the Conservative government. This government boasted through the words of the Prime Minister that it had deliberately induced the current recession. If my memory is correct the Prime Minister not only said that the government deliberately induced this recession but he said that was as clear as spring water.
Canadians will agree that this was in large part the deliberate action of the government due to its high interest rate and high dollar policies. These policies brought this country into a recession ahead of the rest of the world. They also continued the recession longer than might otherwise have been the case.
At the same time that the hon. parliamentary secretary was in effect saying that he and his government deserved mercy for the higher borrowing authority being sought on the grounds of lower government revenues, he was also saying that he and his government deserved credit for what they had accomplished in carrying out their major objective of debt and deficit control.
It is true that when the Conservatives took office they said that bringing the public debt and the deficit under control was among their principal objectives. However the numbers show that in this, as in so many other things, the Conservative government has nothing more than a record of failure.
What is the accumulated public debt today? I was going to say it was $420 billion but I thought I heard the parliamentary secretary say it was in the area of $450 billion. That is more than twice as much as it was when this Conservative government took office. How can this government claim it has achieved its objective of bringing the public debt under control when after eight years of Conservative government that public debt is more than twice as high as when it took office?

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
What about its plea for praise on the grounds that the deficit, the annual difference between revenues and expenditures of the government, is being handled better than when this Conservative government took office?
In his December economic statement the Minister of Finance admitted that the budget deficit for the fiscal year 1992-93 would be $34.4 billion, some $6.9 billion more than had been forecast only a few months previously in his budget of February 1992. The Department of Finance is also saying that the deficit for 1993-94 will be some $10.1 billion above the $22.5 billion estimate contained in that budget of February 1992. If I am not mistaken, the budget deficit at the present time is at about the same place it was when this Conservative government took office. So this government has put the Canadian economy and the Canadian people through a high degree of pain for no real gain.
The government says: "Well, the reason that we have this increase in the public debt and this increase in the deficit is because of the high interest we are paying on our borrowing". Why does the government have to pay such high interest? Why did it have to pay such high interest on its borrowing? It was due to the policy that it helped put in place and supported and sustained for years, a policy of high interest rates which did tremendous damage to the economy of this country and also damaged the fiscal activities of the government itself.
I submit that it is not an accurate and open way of describing the operations of the government for its supporters to say that if we did not look at the interest being paid we would be doing okay. I doubt if that is really accurate, but even if it were, does this make sense to the average household or the average business? They would not say they were doing okay if they did not have to pay interest. Interest is a cost of doing business just as much as is the cost of merchandise or the cost of salaries. Interest is a cost that a household has to take into account, a household that has to make mortgage payments or payments on credit cards. It is just nonsense for the government to try and claim credit from the Canadian people and seek to be praised by the Canadian
people if, as it claims, it would be doing all right if only it did not have to pay such high interest.
In recent months interest rates have, fortunately, come down, but we have to remember that they are still very high in real terms after deducting the rate of inflation. Our interest rates are still very high compared to traditional spreads between interest rates in Canada and interest rates in the United States. While they have come down since the jump up last fall, they are still higher than the low level they reached at the beginning of September. So there is still a long way to go in bringing interest rates down in a way that will bring some real encouragement to this all too weak Canadian economy.
This government is trying to take credit for something which the record shows as an abject failure. When you look at what it said was its primary objective when it took office, the control of the public debt and the deficit, then obviously it has nothing to praise itself for. It stands a failure by the very criterion it set for itself, by the very premise on which it asked to be judged by the Canadian people.
The government, according to the parliamentary secretary, is concerned about the ratio of debt to our gross domestic product. It is now in the area of about 65 per cent. At the time it took office, the ratio of debt to gross domestic product was only 42 per cent. Even looking at this very key measure, we see a serious deterioration in our position compared to the position that existed when this Conservative government took office.
The parliamentary secretary talked about the views of financial institutions and borrowers outside of the country. One of the ways in which this government has made our debt and deficit problem worse than was the case when it took office is the extent to which our debt has come to be held outside this country. When the Conservative government first took office, the debt of the federal government was at least held almost entirely by Canadians. Canadians owed that debt to themselves. Now some 20 per cent or more of that debt is held outside this country, certainly making us more vulnerable than we want to be to outside pressures.
February 4, 1993

This is another reason to criticize this Conservative government when examining its claim for praise on how it achieved its primary objective of bringing our debt and deficit situation under control.
Let me say again that if this government, through the parliamentary secretary or through anyone on the government side of the House, tries to take credit for what has happened with our debt and deficit situation, in effect it is turning reality completely upside down. If this government through the parliamentary secretary or anyone on the government benches attempts to be excused by the Canadian people for the degree of borrowing it needs on the grounds that the weak economy has caused a weakness in government revenues, again I say they are exactly like the person in the story I heard who, when accused of murdering his parents, came before the judge and pleaded for mercy on the grounds that he was an orphan.
What is the effect of Conservative policies on the prospects for the Canadian economy? If we look at the executive summary of the winter Canadian outlook of the Conference Board we will see that while the Conference Board predicts growth in the economy of some 3.3 per cent next year, it also says that our unemployment rates will remain very high. They will remain well above the 11 per cent rate.
The Conference Board says that the most recent economic statement of the Minister of Finance, rather than having a positive effect on the economy, will be of a restrictive nature. The Conference Board said: "The mildly restrictive nature of Finance Minister Mazan-kowski's most recent economic statement will also pull back on growth in 1993".
The Conference Board report goes on to say: "The over-all impact of the measures in that statement will be slightly contractionary, lowering real GDP growth by roughly 0.1 per cent in 1992 and by 0 per cent in 1993". The Conference Board also says: "Consumer spending will be the hardest hit as the most important cost-saving measures were cuts in unemployment insurance benefits and a freeze of Public Service wages".
As the Conference Board points out, when employment growth is weak this obviously discourages people from spending. Surely this helps explain why the recovery is so slow and so weak compared to recoveries from past recessions.
Government Orders
The Department of Finance in its background paper to the budget of last February confirmed that the recovery from the current recession is much weaker than has been the case for any of our previous recessions. It pointed out that the recovery period from the recession of 1981-82 saw growth rates of from 4 per cent to 6 per cent and certainly by 1984 strong recovery had already been having a positive effect on the Canadian economy.
In order to make a real dent in unemployment, in order to bring down unemployment substantially to create the substantial number of new jobs that we must have in order to get well below the 11.6 per cent level we have been seeing and to put hundreds of thousands of Canadians back to work, we need rates of growth well above even the 3.3 per cent predicted by the Conference Board.
We have to get up to the 4 per cent level of growth and above, otherwise we are going to go along as we have been with 1.6 million Canadians out of work with the damage that is doing to their lives, the lives of their families and the lives of their communities across this country.
By the way, it is interesting that while the Conference Board spoke of a forecast of 3 per cent growth next year, this is far more optimistic than the government itself. The Department of Finance in a forecast connected with the economic statement of December by the Minister of Finance talked about growth only at the 2 per cent level. Also, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in a forecast a few weeks ago said that it looked to growth being only at the 2.5 per cent level.
Even if the more optimistic view of the Conference Board turns out to be correct, this will not be enough to bring down unemployment in any substantial way. We see therefore the cumulative and ongoing effects of Conservative economic policy not only in the continued all too high levels of unemployment and the all too low levels of job creation, but also in the figures we saw a few days ago regarding bankruptcies in this country.
The year 1991 was a record year for bankruptcies. Yet this Conservative government outdid itself because the total number of bankruptcies for 1992 set a new record. It was even higher than the record year of 1991.

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
The government says things are not that bad. Bankruptcies went down in December compared to what they were in November, the lowest level in four months. When you compare the number of bankruptcies in December 1992 with the number of bankruptcies in December 1991, they were actually higher than they were a year ago.
How can the government claim any real improvement in the business sector of this country when bankruptcies in December were no better? In fact, they were worse than they were a year ago. This government's policies are causing this country's economy simply to spin its wheels when the economy should be moving forward.
What is troubling about these bankruptcy figures is that the number of business bankruptcies has gone up much more than personal bankruptcies. This is serious. All of these represent tragedies. The increase in business bankruptcies does not augur well for a strong, quick recovery for the return to health of our business sector.
Something else troubling about these numbers is that we see that bankruptcies have actually gone up in three provinces which in the past have been engines of growth for the entire economy. We see that bankruptcies have gone up in British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario. These are provinces to which the rest of the country has often looked for support and strength in terms of a recovery for the entire economy.
These most recent figures for bankruptcies in this countiy are really troubling. They are really a matter of concern when one looks not only at what has been happening but what could be and may well be happening now and over the course of the next year in this country.
We have had some other numbers produced by Statistics Canada. Statistics Canada yesterday published its help wanted index. The help wanted index is often looked on as a bit of a forecast as to what is going to happen to employment in this countiy. This Help wanted index showed no improvement in January at all. In fact, it dropped eight points in Ontario and as well in western Canada. This help wanted index, as members may know, is a survey of help wanted ads in a sample of newspapers across this countiy. This survey, as I have said, does not indicate any real increase or improvement in employment over the coming months.
Similar results can be drawn from a look at the survey of manufacturers which Statistics Canada carried out
and published recently. Statistics Canada questioned thousands of factory operators and owners. The conclusion of this survey, according to a report by Southam News, was that they expected more lay-offs during the next three months.
I want to remind the House that we have already lost
350,000	manufacturing jobs in this country in the past three years. The manufacturing base is crucial not only as a source of employment but as a foundation for the health of the entire economy.
To be fair, I should say that those surveyed expected increased output. More expected increased output than those who expected production to go down, but I repeat, on balance, according to the Southam News report, they expected employment would continue to fall during the next three months, although happily at a slower pace.
This Southam News report by Eric Beauchesne raises a very interesting point. It states:
The survey results again raise questions about claims that a
shortage of skilled workers is as big a problem as the shortage of jobs.
When we question the minister of employment about what is being done to create more jobs, he points to vacancies which need to be filled by skilled people. Certainly there are vacancies which need to be filled by skilled people. That is why we have been pressing the government to take more meaningful action to provide training and upgrading for our work force. However, if every one of those jobs requiring higher levels of skills would be filled, I think it is true to say that there would still be a million or more people out of work in this countiy and that is simply unacceptable. This is something that this government will have to deal with in the remaining few weeks or months that it is in office. Certainly, because it has not dealt with this problem, when the next election comes it is not going to continue in office.
What we have to recognize is that we not only need higher degrees of skill on the part of our work force, we need more jobs. There simply are not enough jobs in this country for the hundreds of thousands of people who want to work. We need policies whereby the government will work with the provinces and the private sector to create more jobs. We have to get away from the destructive policies of this government which have destroyed jobs rather than created them, which have driven businesses into bankruptcy rather than helping business to be healthy and to expand and move forward.
February 4, 1993

We need different policies than the policies of this government which have driven this country into the worst recession since the 1930s and have taken away hope and optimism from Canadians and replaced it with despair about the future. Canadians deserve better from their federal government, even from this Conservative government. They deserve much better than they obviously have received.
This government has asked, through the parliamentary secretary, for approval of a higher level of borrowing. I suppose it is true that as with business, government revenues do not always match the timing of its expenditures and governments have to borrow. However the parliamentary secretary has certainly not made a convincing case on behalf of the economic record and economic policies of this government.
A few weeks ago we were startled to hear an announcement by Statistics Canada that the recession was over. Canadians reacted to that announcement with consternation. Were there still not 1.6 million people out of work? Were businesses not announcing day after day thousands more lay-offs in coming weeks and months? Were businesses not announcing that they were going into receivership and closing factories and stores? No wonder Canadians were astounded by this announcement. No wonder there was no dancing in the streets and throwing hats in the air.
While technically it may be that the recession is over, the fact is that this is unfortunately only in the most technical sense, in the sense that perhaps the economy is no longer contracting and there are some signs of growth and movement.
How can we say we are in a recovery when there are still more than 1.6 million people out of work? Some of the so-called experts on the government side say that yes, it is a recovery but unfortunately a jobless recovery. What a contradiction in terms. How can there be a recovery in the economy of this country while there are still 1.6 million people out of work?
For the people who are out of work the recession is not over, in my own city of Windsor or anywhere else in this country, until people are back to work at permanent and
Government Orders
satisfying jobs. For them, no matter what the government says or any of its experts and spokespersons say, the recession continues and the recovery is not really here while we have so many people out of work.
I would like to see a strong recovery under way. I take no real satisfaction out of noting the despair and the lack of hope on the part of hundreds of thousands of Canadians. I take no real satisfaction out of noting the continued statistics about unemployment, bankruptcy and economic weakness, but this is the reality.
I have an obligation on the part of the people of my community and on the part of Canadians generally to say what is really going on. The government can take no satisfaction from any declaration by Statistics Canada that the recession is over while more than 1.6 million people are out of work and respected forecasting organizations like the Conference Board say that they have little or no prospect of going back to work for a year and more.
We need a different approach to government, an approach which recognizes problems of debt and deficit but which at the same time has a commitment to economic growth and which recognizes the contribution which only economic growth can make both to the creation of jobs and yes, the containment of our debt and the controlling of our deficit.
As even the parliamentary secretary admitted when he presented third reading of this bill to the House, when you have recession and worse, governments must spend money on things like unemployment insurance and welfare and at the same time government revenues decline because people are not working. They have no salaries so they pay no taxes. At current levels of growth government revenues decrease. Businesses do not make profits and they do not pay taxes either. However, in a context of economic growth governments spend less on things like unemployment insurance and welfare. People who are working and businesses that are making profits, without any higher tax burden, are the source of higher revenues for government. Economic growth itself is a major tool, a major instrument in the control and containment and ultimately the rolling back of the public debt and the deficit.

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
At the same time economic growth provides the jobs required for satisfying lives for Canadians. Economic growth provides the basis for hope for the future, the confidence that there will be a better future for Canadians and their families.
This government deserves a severe indictment and, more important, a severe penalty from the Canadian people because, getting beyond the statistics, getting beyond the numbers, the fact is it has robbed millions of Canadians of their hope for the future. It has robbed millions of Canadians of the confidence they deserve to have and better lives for themselves and their families.
I say that we look forward to an early election so that the Canadian people will pass judgement on this government, remove it from office and give a new and better government a place in this House and this country. I believe it will be a Liberal government, one that will bring back hope and confidence for Canadians and help us to build a country worthy of its past and worthy of its future.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in this debate. The Conservative government is asking the people for authority through this House to borrow another $8 billion.
This debate offers a rare opportunity to talk about the continuing tragedy of the Canadian nation. What we have just witnessed today is a speech from the finance critic of the Liberal Party that could be found in the library, given by the Conservative Party when it was in opposition. This back and forth of blame between Conservatives and Liberals in the history of this country politically was once explained as the difference between, as Tommy Douglas said, tweedledee and tweedledum.
When they are in government they are tweedledum. When they are in opposition they are tweedledee.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: The tweedledummers are in opposition.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: The tweedledums are in government and the tweedledees are in opposition.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: You have not got a hope.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: No, it does not matter. The cast of characters are essentially the same old record of attacking each other without offering positive alternatives or explaining to the Canadian people how they will get out of this mess.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Tell us about Bob Rae.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I appreciate the interruptions made by both the Liberals and the Conservatives. It is guilt motivated and were I one of the priesthood, I would say forgive them for they know not what they do. In actual fact they indeed know what they do and they continue to repeat the same errors over and over again.
When the Conservatives ran for office they damned vociferously the debt and the deficits left by the Liberal Party. They promised that they would reduce the debt and the operating deficits. Just vote for a government under the Tories and all the problems will be resolved. Eight years later the same annual deficits are cropping up plus more demands for borrowing.
The gall is even worse for the Canadian taxpayers when they hear the Liberal Party suggest it has the answers when it left a massive debt and massive deficits when it was in power.
Tweedledee or tweedledum, take your pick. Neither has shown the innovation that the Canadian people demand. Less than 30 million people in this great nation have a cornucopia of resources, a cornucopia of wealth in terms of the ordinary people, the labour force, entrepreneurs and no leadership that is dramatic or imaginative enough to put together a package to pull this country up by its own bootstraps.
It is well enough for the members of the Official Opposition to look at the Gallup polls and see that they are leading. They decided the best approach is to come into this House and attack the government and say: "we will do better, trust us". They need to do more than that. It is the obligation of the Liberals to say exactly what they will do, not just stand up in this House and condemn the government. I too will present some ideas.
February 4, 1993

It is a dereliction of duty for the Liberal Party to come into this House and not tell us exactly where it stands on the GST, on the free trade agreement and on NAFTA.
The Liberals need to be concerned and heckled but I want to say right now that any suggestion that the Liberals go into the next election without defining where they stand on the GST and leaving the impression they will tax food must be put in writing as either a truth or a lie. They cannot escape the obligation to tell the Canadian people where they are coming from before the next election.
We know that the Tories have been failures. We know that they have philosophically pursued a course of action that has brought about devastation in this country. Built on that failure is a tacit implication that the Liberals will follow most of the Tory policies with minor changes. If we are going to make that suggestion then what we end up with is exactly this: A vote for the Liberals is a vote for the Tories.
A deficit of $35 billion caused by what? Yes, part of the explanation in my opinion was correct by the Liberal finance critic. Economic growth has been stifled. Yes, there has been a recession. However, part of the reason for the stifling of that economic growth has been the free trade agreement which has allowed Canada to lose jobs in the manufacturing base at three times the rate of what the Americans have.
Did the Liberals say they will cancel the free trade agreement? No, they will tinker with it. I will say right now that we would give the six months' notice of abrogation and that is on record. That is what politics is all about, to say clearly and honestly where you stand. I stand here and say that the New Democratic Party would cancel the free trade agreement by giving the six months' notice.
One must say honestly that the Tories are touting this as their policy and they support it. The New Democrats say it is wrong and we would cancel. What is more dangerous is that the Official Opposition refuses to say what side of the issue it is on with the free trade agreement.
The Canadian people have a right and an obligation to know exactly what they are voting for and voting against. If you want the free trade agreement, vote for the Conservatives. If you do not want it, vote New Demo-
Govemment Orders
crat. If you do not know what you want except licking your finger and holding it up in the wind, vote for the Liberal Party.
I want to talk about the North America free trade agreement. I think the Tories are wrong. We agree in principle that they are wrong on this issue. There will be further erosion of the job base, causing more borrowing such as this bill. Where does the Liberal Party stand on the North American free trade agreement? Traditionally where it always has: North American free trade if necessary but not necessarily North American free trade.
Contradictory statements allow the Liberals to play both sides against the middle. We have a disillusioned public that is fed up with politics and politicians and they want a change of government.
Instead of giving leadership, the Liberal Party is back on the fence again. It created these debts and deficits. Now members make these swan-song speeches about how terrible it is, the Tories have done wrong but do not worry, big business will carry on the same old policies.
There has been a massive shift of taxation in this country away from the business sector, away from the corporate sector and on to ordinary people. Did the Liberals say they will put it back in a fair tax policy? In a pig's eye, they will. We cannot get three logical words of commitment from the Liberal leader when asked about tax policy. Have you ever heard of a man running for prime minister who stands up publicly and says he will tell us what he is going to do after he has won? That is like playing dice with the Damon Runyan character Harry the Horse. He throws the dice in the hat, holds it up over his head and calls out the numbers.
We do not need pig in the poke policies. We need honest statements by everybody in this House of what they intend to do to get this country out of the mess. The Tories have failed. They are gone. Nothing is going to save them.
The Liberals have an obligation to be honest with the Canadian people. Up to this date they have not been. They have an opportunity on this bill to tell the truth and they have not done so.
If you want Tory policies, vote for the Tories. For goodness' sake do not have a Liberal Party hiding behind Tory policy saying: "Oh, they are bad. Oh, they are wrong. When the Liberals get elected they will not change a dam thing.

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
Why do they not take memberships out in the Tory party because the Tories are doing the Liberals' dirty work for them while the Liberals are hiding behind the curtains on these issues.
Why do we not have a clear-cut statement from the Liberal Party? January 1, 1994 is the implementation date of the North American free trade agreement. Regardless of how the Liberals vote in this House, regardless of talking about renegotiating or abrogation, we are talking about a new feature, implementation date January 1, 1994.
The election will be held before then. The people of this country have a right to know. If you vote Liberal will they refuse to implement the agreement on January 1, 1994? We know where the Tories stand. They will implement. However, this polling is directly related to the loss of jobs because of those trade agreements and we have not had a statement from the Liberal Party to the Canadian people that it will not implement on January 1, 1994.
Liberals cannot hide forever. The Canadian people are fed up to the teeth with duplicity, dodging and weaving. As much as I disagree with the Tories, as much as disdain their policies but like them as persons, it is in my charitable nature to love all people. It is my charitable nature to love all people and respect the rules of this House more than anything else. Even though I love some Liberals as individuals, hypocrisy cannot and must not be allowed to play a part in the forthcoming election in this country.
We hear the Liberals saying naughty, naughty to the Tories. Do we hear the Liberals say that the corporations must pay their fair share so that we avoid this kind of debt? Not on your life. Do we hear the Liberals saying we will never take 10 cents from a big corporation so that we can implement policies?
We read the records of who gave money to the Liberal Party. It is listed in the accounts of corporations and banks that gave money to the Liberal Party. It is all there.
My dear friends in the Liberal Party think they can have it both ways. This government has been a failure. It is going to be thrown out of office. You cannot be thrown in on the basis of fooling the Canadian people. Come clean and tell us where you stand on the GST. Where do you stand on the free trade agreement? Will you implement the North American free trade agreement in 1994?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: How about wage controls?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
What are some options? I have a few comments to make. My friend mentioned wage controls. I was the only premier in Canada who refused to accept the Liberal policy of wage controls. I went back to British Columbia and implemented a policy of price controls- under a Liberal government, and we should never forget that. Price controls on food and energy, so that ordinary people could be protected from rapacious federal governments.
Let us look at the expenditure of public funds. This bill forces us again to borrow and add on to the debt for our children and our children's children. It is the same old kind of borrowing that both the Liberals and Conservatives are committed to: making offshore lenders wealthier yet based on the 27 or 28 million taxpayers in this country who are indebted offshore and internally in massive amounts.
There has never been a serious attempt since the Second World War to mobilize indigenous Canadian capital to work in Canada for Canadians. Canadians are among the best savers in the world. During the Second World War, capital as an instrument was mobilized just as much as manpower and arms were mobilized to fight for the success and survival of democracy. Everybody sacrificed, everybody contributed. Imaginative options were created in the financial sector during wartime which permitted this country to move rapidly out of the depression into measured and sustained growth.
I know it is a four letter word that frightens the Liberals and the Conservatives plan. The Japanese plan an economy, the Germans plan an economy and the new administration in the United States is now going to plan an economy. The new president admitted it yesterday. Not the Liberal Party or the Conservatives-laissez-faire forever.
What are the options? One is to examine those Canadian savings. This government finally opened up a very small window of access to those accumulated savings. A very good policy initiating self-responsibility in savings with tax benefits was opened to the Canadian people under the RRSP program. Good for the Liberals, they brought it in. It gave ordinary people an option to protect themselves against both inflation and devaluation of their own hard-earned money in high tax times by moving it into RRSPs.
February 4, 1993

Currently there is $105 billion in RRSP money in this country. Half of it is in self-directed funds and the other half is not.
There are ideas out there begging to be implemented that have absolutely nothing to do with the Tories, the Liberals or the New Democrats. They are strange to politicians, they are under the heading of common sense. One of those common sense ideas has been presented by the Canadian Federation of Municipalities calling for access to low cost funds to rebuild the infrastructure of this country; roads, sewers, sidewalks, all jobs that do not require a Ph.D.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: The Liberals did not show up for the vote.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I talk about the need for higher education for jobs. Just recently the most highly skilled work force in all of Canada was laid off in Ottawa in the high-tech industry. The high-tech myth is a Lorelei that is used by politicians to suck people along into thinking there is a great future there. Not everybody has a Ph.D. Thank God for that. Not everybody has a university education. Simple, clear-cut manufacturing jobs and industrial related jobs are the foundation of a resource based economy such as we have in Canada. However, it takes leadership.
Of that $104 or $105 billion that exists in the RRSP funds, as I pointed out, half of it is not directed. With wisdom, prudence, caution and leadership, using the Canadian municipal federation's own plans, municipal bonds could be issued tax free based on the United States model of the Fannie Mae municipal bonds.
The municipalities have said that there is $15 billion worth of work that should be initiated right away. We should allow people the choice, the freedom and the option to subscribe to a government bond that pays two points less than the going rate available in treasury bills or other securities and allow them to buy those bonds directly from their RRSP funds. We should allow them to give 10 or 20-year commitments to those bonds, within the shelter of the RRSP, to protect all interest they earn on those bonds and allow them to take that interest out tax free at the time the commitment is over, be they either 20-year bonds or 10-year bonds.

The consultation process would be extensive and would then lead to the alternative to the present tax system which as you know, Madam Speaker, is tilted very much in favour of the haves and is heavier on the have nots.
In other words, what we intend to do after the next election is have a more progressive taxation system with hopefully less flat tax rates applied regardless of income and with rates of taxation which are heavier on those who have more and which are of course progressively
lighter as incomes decrease. That is the Liberal view on the approach to taxation. We know that can be done.
Since 1984 there have been over 30 tax increases introduced by the present government. We will have to look at all of them and reorganize the taxation system in a fair and progressive manner.

I will attempt to divide these remarks between water and energy, fully aware of the fact that the subject is so

immense that it cannot be covered adequately by way of just one intervention.

The pesticides are as a result of a decision made by this government regarding packages costing $500 or more. If they are labelled in accordance with the pest control products regulations, having a purpose that includes agricultural use, they will be exempt from the GST.
I ask why on earth the government would take a step of this kind. Certainly it is a measure which will facilitate an increase in the use of pesticides. We know that some of the pesticides in commercial use are extremely damaging to the environment and particularly to the water systems.
One cannot help but ask this question. Why should books not be exempt from the GST when chemical fertilizers are exempt? What is the rationale behind this initiative? Why would the government do that when in the green plan, which is certainly not under the jurisdiction of Treasury Board but nevertheless is part of the over-all long-term approach of this government, there is a profound concern about the preservation and the protection of the environment. Here we have an indirect subsidy, an exemption from a tax which applies to a product which we all know ought to be used extremely carefully and possibly phased out in the long term. The federal water strategy was in a way launched by way of an initiative by the Liberal government before the 1984 election which set up a water commission under the leadership of Professor Pearse at UBC.
I believe that commission reported in 1985 or 1986. In 1987 a federal water strategy emerged and we welcomed it. We thought it was a good idea. It is a good idea because we need a federal water strategy for a variety of reasons. The only unfortunate aspect of that strategy was the fact that it remained silent on water diversion and water exports. That was because at that time some members of the Conservative government were in favour of some of the crazy ideas being proposed for massive water diversions between Canada and the United States.
That federal water strategy has remained virtually unimplemented. A federal water bill has been promised by several successive ministers of the environment. Here we see an increasing need for a policy to be implemented in the interest of public health of Canadians and the long-term use of water which is being recognized increasingly as a commodity of increasing and substantive importance, not just in Canada but around the globe. A legitimate question to be raised during this debate would be when will this promise be delivered?

chemicals is still entering that river. We learned that of these 18 toxic chemicals, eight are still unregulated. In other words, there is no regulation affecting eight of these 18 persistent toxic chemicals as of today.

speechtext: I will read the "blues" and if necessary come back to the House on this point.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is with a certain amount of chagrin that I rise to join in this debate today. It is an honour for me to follow such experienced and illustrious members of this House as the hon. member for Davenport and the hon. member for Windsor West.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Excuse me.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I do not know why the hon. Solicitor General wants to be excused, but I will excuse him if he wishes.
In a discussion with the hon. member for Windsor West earlier this morning he made a point that I agree with whole-heartedly. He said in a borrowing bill such as the one we are debating today it is tantamount to irresponsibility of the highest order to give the government that has so mismanaged the Canadian economy over the last eight years another crack at it by giving it any more money. This government should realize what it has done and is doing to the Canadian people. Throw in the towel and do what the Canadian people want, which is call an election and call it today. No more borrowing bills. No more money to the government.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Increasing the debt.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Issue the writ.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: The public knows this is not an alternative.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Canadian people do not mind. I love the way the hon. member from Manitoba hurls an insult and leaves just as I love the way the hon. Solicitor General keeps wanting to be excused. I have excused him. He can go.
Let us look at some of the things this government has done to the people of Canada over the last eight years.
Government Orders
In this year of grace alone the deficit has been revised from $27.5 billion to $34.4 billion. For average Canadians worried about their jobs, worried about their children's education, worried about whether their children will ever have a job, worried about whether they are going to have a job next week and worried about the economy generally, it is really wonderful to hear that the deficit has been, and I quote those anaemic not to say banal words, revised upward. It sounds so unthreatening to say that something has been revised upwards.
If we take $27.5 billion from $34.4 billion then we have a huge increase in the deficit from a government that has told us from the day of its arrival in power, a day that shall live in infamy, September 4, 1984, that it was going to deal with the deficit. It certainly dealt with the deficit. Oh, yes. We cannot deny that it has dealt with the deficit, revising it upward and upward every year, every day, every month. Every morning Canadians wake up and they are another $100 million in debt.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Shame. Shame.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
This is the government that wants to borrow more money and take us further into debt. This is the government that is looking for voters' confidence. It is amazing. This is a government that with this kind of record could not get a car loan from a chartered bank.
This same government over eight years has attacked and attacked the fabric of this country and the dreams of Canadians. It has attacked the simple things that every Canadian thought were his or her heritage.
It is absolutely appalling to look at the fiscal record of this government. It is appalling to think that in the 1990s Canadians are as ill-prepared for the future and in as bad a position financially as they are when we are facing the exigencies of the globalization of our economy.
It is beyond belief that a government that has created this snafu, that has created situations in which Canadians no longer feel that there is any hope for the future or that they can trust their government, then comes out with a whole load of theories that are tired and do nothing for individual Canadians. The government does not do the one thing that every Canadian from coast to coast to coast wants it to do: deal with the economy and create some real jobs.

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
That is what Canadians want in every riding in this country. Whether it is one of the major Toronto ridings, such as Broadview-Greenwood or Scarborough, smaller ridings in Ontario, ridings in the greater Montreal area, such as Saint-Laurent, Halifax, western Canada, central Canada, northern Canada, urban or rural does not matter.
What do Canadians want? We know what they want. They want jobs. They do not want jobs at fast food outlets that pay them minimum wage. They want jobs that give them hope for the future. They want jobs that give them a chance to provide for their families. They want jobs that give them a decent standard of living. That is the birthright of Canadians. What has this government done? It has taken away their birthright.
Not to pour oil on the fire, I am afraid that attitude is a stupid attitude. In this House, no matter where we sit, we must understand, as our neighbours to the south have understood and as maybe the Solicitor General who still needs to be excused will understand some day, that it is the economy.
There was a phrase said in the United States that I hesitate to use here in this House. I think we all know what it was. It is the economy. It has been the economy. It will continue to be the economy. It is the economy for every man, woman and child in this country. It has become a truism that the best social policy is a job.
In this country today young people come out of training courses, universities and vocational schools and they cannot get jobs. Whether they are trained to be skilled workers, whether they have a Ph.D., a law degree, an MD, an MBA, or a degree in engineering they cannot get a job. There are young people in this country today who have gone five, six, or seven years without anything that remotely approaches a real job. That is a disgrace.
That is something that every one of us should be giving our best efforts toward solving. In this country young people work hard, study hard, learn everything they can and get themselves trained but then there is nothing for them when they come out.
I do not know how many of us in this House have ever gone through a significant period of unemployment. I did once, very briefly. It was about a three-month period. I well remember the feeling of not being able to find a job.
I remember the depression when one realizes that with one's skills and education one still cannot find a job. In this country today there are millions of people in that situation.
What is their government doing for them? Zip. Nothing. What is it doing for those people who have looked to the government for assistance? Nothing. This is not something that any Canadian of whatever political stripe can deal with. This is not something that they should have to deal with. This is something that calls for immediate action.
It is interesting watching our neighbour to the south, the things that happen, the desire for change that is roiling across this country as it roiled across the United States in the most recent election.
We look at President Clinton's announcement yesterday that he is going to immediately introduce an infrastructure rebuilding program. Is that not interesting?

speechtext: You should have been here last night to vote.

The point is that the President of the United States will introduce an immediate infrastructure package. Who has been saying that in this House for two years?
