He has been saying that, as have all of us in the Liberal Official Opposition-as opposed to those persons who have no official status and keep interrupting, and I promise the hon. Solicitor General that it will become more official as the sparks fly upward or should I say as the flames engulf-they are burning in Orillia right now.
February 4, 1993

At any rate, the point is that jobs, jobs, jobs are the answer. We know that is the answer. The time has come to do something about it. The time has come to relieve the anxiety and the out and out fear that is grabbing Canadians by the throat. The time has come for this government to do what governments are supposed to do in this country.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Resign.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I agree with that too. However, if this government is not going to do what it should do, which is issue the writ now as we are four years and two months past the date of the last election, then it should create jobs for Canadians. That is what this government should do. Creating the climate for a good economy is what Canadian governments-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Climate.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I do not disagree with the hon. minister. He is saying to me "climate" and he is shaking his finger.
I agree with him. Do it.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Not create jobs.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
You could create a few jobs too. It has happened in the 126-year history of this country that now and again the federal government has tried to create a few jobs, though I admit not often in the last eight years.
Other governments have created jobs. The sky has not fallen and the capitalist system has not fallen into the ocean. Creating jobs, if it happens to be a by-product of creating the climate to create jobs, is not necessarily a bad thing for the people of this country, particularly when the people of this country are attempting to wend their way out of the worst recession since the Great Depression of the 1930s.
We are sitting here in this House today in one of the coldest winters physically and economically that Canadians have ever seen. There is rank and abject suffering out there in this country while we sit here in this House and see no programs being developed to assist people.
Instead we see the creation of institutionalized attacks on Canadian citizens. I refer to Bill C-105, which I understand is not going to be debated today. One can only hope that the government is seeing the error of its ways. I want to talk about that because if the government is not seeing the error of its ways maybe it needs a few stories with human faces about what this bill could do to
Government Orders
the people of Canada if it is left as it was originally introduced.
When I first questioned the government on this bill before Christmas I mentioned the horrors facing Canadian working people who will no longer have the opportunity to be protected by the Unemployment Insurance Act if they quit "voluntarily".
From 1980 to 1984 I chaired the unemployment insurance appeal board in Halifax. I saw many cases of people who quit because of horrendous working conditions. The one I remember most was a man who was working-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: That is justification.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I am getting to that.
I understand about justification. If the member will just be a little patient he will see the point to my story.
There was a man who quit his job and was disqualified by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. He came before us as the appeal board to explain the reason that he had quit. He was working on an underground project. Subterranean piping was being put in. It was winter and it was cold. He was wearing rubber protective clothing but because of the temperature in the hole in the ground in which he was working the rubber would freeze and it was very difficult to move. On top of that water from some place or other was pouring down his neck while he was working. He said that he just could not stay there. He was sick every night, he was getting a cold, he was going to get pneumonia and on and on.
In that particular case we allowed the appeal. It went on to the umpire and it lost. The umpire did not want to deny the appeal but said he was forbidden to allow it because of the provisions of the act.
If that situation is not sufficient to create just cause everyone of us can think of thousands of other situations in which working people are going to be at a disadvantage because of employers.
In the entire UI appeals process employers do not even have to show up. The person who has left his job goes to the appeal. If the employer does not want to show up, and it is nothing to the employer, he does not have to come. What about-and I am not going to discuss it to any great extent because I have talked about it before and I will talk about it again in a different context-the whole question of sexual harassment?

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
The Minister of Employment and Immigration responded by saying that sexual harassment is just cause. That is cods wallop. It is not just cause.
This government, this country and this culture do not yet truly recognize that sexual harassment is a creation of offensive behaviour against women. The vast majority of men still do not understand the point. The fact that women are forced to deal with what can only be described as an unfair burden of proof means that they are not going to get their just desserts under this bill. This is just another example of the way in which this government carries on cavalierly in the face of evidence to the contrary and attacks working people rather than creating the right climate, as much as the minister might not like it, and creating some jobs so that people can have a decent life.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: They do not care.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I am afraid the hon. member for Kent is absolutely right. The Conservatives do not care. They will care soon. Within the next six months they will care, but by then it will be too late.
There are so many tragedies developing in this county1 from coast to coast. In my region of Atlantic Canada tragedies in the field of employment, and the lack thereof, are becoming so much the order of the day that they almost do not have any impact any more. People are becoming callous because tragedy is something they deal with eveiy day.
The situation in Port Hawkesbury-am I out of time? I will leave the situation in Port Hawkesbury and just say that this is something the government could work on as well.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was probably one of the few people in the House who listened to my hon. friend's remarks. I did so because she represents a maritime riding and the estimates include moneys which will go, in part, toward the purchase of the new helicopters.
We have all sat here and listened in amazement as her leader attacked the fisherpersons of this country and attacked the military by saying that the Liberal Party when it is elected would eliminate or cancel the plans for these new helicopters.
In view of the fact that these new helicopters will be used in search and rescue missions, which is very
important to my hon. friend's electorate, and in view of the fact that she has a military component among her electors I wonder if my hon. friend would like to take this opportunity to disassociate herself completely from the remarks of her leader, or does she want to suggest that her electors want to fly about in these 30-year old helicopters that will be 35 years old by the time they are replaced? This has been a devastating attack on people who require helicopters for rescue.
I notice my hon. friend did not participate in any of the questioning on the helicopter issue. I would have thought she would have, unless she really rejected her leader's position on this purchase. It would be good for her to set the record straight. She should start her personal election campaign by abandoning that position. Those helicopters are so old they have almost served longer than the Leader of the Official Opposition and they run the veiy real risk of becoming older than some of her leader's ideas.
I thought it would be appropriate to take this time to put on the record the fact that the member should abandon her leader's old ideas, abandon this nonsense about the helicopters and stand up for her electors in Halifax.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it always gives me great joy to be questioned by the hon. Solicitor General because he gives me such wonderful material.
I am going to deal with the helicopters, but let me first say that I stood up for my electors about the possibility of putting the women's prison in the greater Halifax-Dart-mouth area, where the facilities are. However the Solicitor General put it in Truro, where there are no facilities. That is all right. I am sure the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester was happy but I do not know about the hon. member for Halifax West.
Allow me to deal with the helicopters. Disassociate myself from my leader? Never. First, Liberals do not do that and, second, my leader is right.
In my riding there is not just a significant military component, as the Solicitor General called it, but the largest military base in the country and we are very proud of that. We are proud of the search and rescue and we are proud of the Sea Kings, which may be old but they do the job. If they were refit and refurbished they could continue to do the job. It is only elderly solicitor generals who have a problem with being over 35.
February 4, 1993

Another very interesting point is that I have another component in my riding. In my riding and close to my riding I have five universities with the highest tuitions, the oldest physical plants and the lowest salaries in Canada. Why do we have this problem in our universities in Atlantic Canada and in my riding of Halifax? One of the reasons is the cuts this government has made to Established Programs Financing, and more so the cuts it has made to R and D.
The five universities in the greater Halifax area heard the Leader of the Opposition say that we would priorize moneys that would have been wasted on nuclear search helicopters that we do not need. I have a news flash for the government: the nuclear threat has reduced and the cold war is over. My leader said that he would priorize that spending and direct it into, among other things, research and development at Canadian universities.
At Dalhousie University, the Technical University of Nova Scotia, St. Mary's University, the Atlantic School of Theology, the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design and at my Alma Mater, which is outside my riding but on the edge of it, Mount St. Vincent University, people cheered when they heard that because they want more research and development. That is what we need and that is what this government will not give us.
If the Solicitor General is so interested in the helicopters can I also remind him about the submarines. His government was going to give us all these submarines.
When I was nominated in 1988 I built my nomination speech around the fact that we did not need or want submarines. Lo and behold I got elected and I am here now. It did not hurt me then and I suggest to the hon. Solicitor General that the people of Halifax know what is smart defence spending and what is not smart defence spending. They will be very happy when we have control of those kinds of budgets and we spend the money in places where it can be best utilized.

I remind my honourable, very kind and truly gallant friend from Sault Ste. Marie that I am awfully sorry we were not here last night. Believe me, if ever in the history of the world right after pigs fly they form a national government, I will be happy to support their infrastructure project.

The Liberal Party is laying claim to what was instituted by the Minister of Finance with regard to housing policy as its ideas. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I say to the hon. minister that I am delighted to give credit where credit is due. I have even given some of it to his government.
I would like to add in closing that I wish the Conservatives would steal some more good ideas from anywhere so we could have a few decent programs that the people of this country so desperately need.
The hon. minister could steal a couple more good ideas. I will give them to him, and if he would implement them quickly and create some jobs I would not care if he ever thanked me. As a matter of fact I would not care if he did not even mention my name.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are obviously debating the borrowing authority bill. It is quite interesting from the contradictions in the speech of the member for Halifax that she represents the party that is famous for its spending and overspending and famous for not attacking anything or going after any measure that would reduce our debt as a country. The Liberals are for spending more; they are never for spending less.
With regard to some of the specifics she mentioned when she talked about the government creating jobs, I think it is worth mentioning that the point we on this side of the House should make more often is that a government puts in place policies and legislation that create an atmosphere or a climate wherein jobs are created. Her solution is to borrow more money and throw more money at the problem, without attacking the very shaky policies they have had over the years that have created some of the problems we now face. If borrowing more money was a solution to the problem all governments would do it.
There is failed logic in the speech just given by the member for Halifax. She attacked the very thing they have supported for years and years.
A government has to get the fundamentals correct. It has to create a climate wherein people want to invest, businessmen want to take chances, and real jobs are created. I will go through some of the elements that must be present to create real jobs.
I remind the member there are 1.3 million more Canadians working today than when we took office. That is an established fact. There are over 12 million Canadians in the work force. Incidentally those 12 million Canadians in the work force-Canadians who are working today is the way I should phrase it-represent 89 per cent of all Canadians eligible to work who are working. We do have an unemployment rate which is higher than any of us in this House would like to see, but we still have 89 per cent of all Canadians working.
Obviously we would like to achieve 100 per cent. Can we achieve it? Maybe we can, but we achieve it by supporting the types of programs and the types of strategy we on this side of the House support. I want to remind the member what some of those programs are and what we have done with regard to the fundamentals.
Interest rates would be a good place to start. Some 10 years ago perhaps all of us in the House were in the work force, but Canada had 20 per cent interest rates under the leadership of a Liberal government. Interest rates went through the roof; inflation went through the roof.
In Canada today we have the lowest inflation rate we have had in 20 years. We have the lowest interest rates we have had in 20 years. This fosters a climate for investment and is why Canada is predicted to lead the G-7 nations in economic growth this year.
The fundamentals are there and they are working. They are going to create real jobs and real opportunity. That is what we on this side of the House believe.

February 4, 1993

Mr. Speaker, it may be possible that I will not be here to participate in the debate on the fixed link project so I want to make my views and my strong support known for this 13-kilometre bridge.
As a member of Parliament and businessman in Atlantic Canada for years, I know for sure that the key to Atlantic Canada's economic future lies in the best possible transportation system available. Without proper highways and without this direct connection to the Island, we will never achieve our potential and share in the wealth of Canada.
Currently Prince Edward Island has an unemployment rate almost 40 per cent higher than that of New Brunswick or Nova Scotia. It also has a much lower average income. I believe that when the fixed link is completed, Prince Edward Island will be able to compete on a level playing field with the other maritime provinces. This, combined with a proper four-lane highway throughout the region, will allow the entire area to compete with anyone.
Not only will this project provide a competitive infrastructure, it will also attract hundreds of thousands of tourists to our area during construction and after completion. In the meantime it will create thousands of jobs throughout the Atlantic region in a time when we need them the most.
For those of us in the immediate area it is hard to believe that the project is actually about to begin. The concept of a fixed link has been talked about for a hundred years and even as late as two decades ago approaches were-
The hon. member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, Progressive Conservative members from Quebec have once again ignored the needs of their fellow citizens by voting against a motion condemning as unfair, inequitable and far too severe a government policy that introduces cuts in unemployment insurance.
They continue to add to the already heavy burden on people who are in greatest need. They forget they have a duty to defend the interests of their fellow citizens who are barely coping in these difficult times. We must remember that when people lose their jobs and are not eligible for benefits, they have to go on welfare, which means the burden is shifted to the provinces.
We must also remember that the government administers a fund to which it does not contribute one penny. Since only employers and employees pay into the fund, they should at least have some say in the matter and have a chance to consider their future.

Mr. Speaker, when the talking stops and action is required Canadians cannot find the Liberal Party.
The Liberals have changed their position on free trade. The Liberals have changed their position on the GST. On the gulf war they had three different positions over three different days.
Last night, when the House voted on an infrastructure and highways program, the Liberals did not attend the vote. The Liberals knew about the vote. Only six Liberal MPs showed up to support the motion presented by the NDP member for Regina-Lumsden, calling for a national infrastructure program and a highways program.
On 15 occasions since last November the Liberal Party has asked for such a program in this House. Yet last night, when there was a vote on this motion, the Liberals did not attend. Had they attended last night's motion, it would have passed.

February 4, 1993

Mr. Speaker, today Le Devoir reports that the Ecole superieure de danse du Quebec in Montreal has informed its teachers and accompanists that there has been a change in policy and they will be obliged to work during a summer course held from June 21 to July 23.
The existing jurisprudence and unemployment insurance manuals refer to section 6.2(5): failure to renew a job contract. According to this section, most teaching contracts are automatically renewed from year to year. A teacher quits voluntarily if he decides not to renew his contract for the coming year.
Fifty per cent of the income of the Ecole de danse du Quebec comes from provincial subsidies. Here we see employers already tightening the screws before Bill C-105 has even been adopted. They are trying to intimidate employees into signing a contract for the summer so they can make more money. At this rate, we must have some amendments to Bill C-105.

Mr. Speaker, children and adults in Davis Inlet have reached the depth of despair when attempts are made to end their lives.
There are 100 of these communities in Canada. We have a Third World problem within our own country. The pattern of disease among Canada's aboriginal people resembles the main killers of the developing world.
As Canada's legislators in this House of Commons we have a moral responsibility to take serious constructive action to address these critical problems. I cannot accept members in this House declaring that this situation is the fiduciary responsibility of a certain province or another. We can no longer allow the aboriginal community to be the ping-pong ball in the jurisdictional debate between the federal government and the provinces.
For years we have been hearing what needs to be done and how we can do it, yet we have continued to
procrastinate. The economic and cultural base of native communities needs strengthening immediately. Action is needed now, not further study.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend our government and the province of Alberta for their co-operative efforts in signing the Canada-Alberta Environmentally Sustainable Agriculture Agreement.
The goal is to facilitate the conservation and protection of the natural resources that agriculture uses to minimize the impact of agriculture on the environment.
As the member for Wild Rose I applaud both the spirit of co-operation between the two levels of government and the long-range view toward protecting the agricultural environment of Alberta.

Mr. Speaker, this government just does not get it. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development keeps saying relocation of the Davis Inlet Innu is not the answer.
The minister does not understand the difference between a relocation forced on a people and a relocation requested by a people. Sending the children outside their home territory for treatment when they have to return to the same despair and hopelessness they are trying to escape is no solution.
Why will the government not believe the Innu when they say relocation to the site they have chosen on the mainland is their best hope for the fresh new beginning they so desperately need in order to heal themselves?
Time and time again aboriginal people in this country have suffered the consequences of government presuming to know what is best for their interests. This attitude has to stop now.
The government does not know what is best for the Innu. I urge the government to trust the Innu to propose the right solutions for their people. Listen to them and respond. Do not impose outside solutions. The Innu cannot take it any more and we will not stand for it.
February 4, 1993

Mr. Speaker, yesterday we saw the spectacle of an Official Opposition depending on political rhetoric and disinformation to satisfy its own partisan ends.
Just now we heard the hon. member for Gatineau-La Lievre say that the federal government does not participate in any way in the Unemployment Insurance Fund. To a certain extent this is true, but it is not the whole truth, because the federal government has an obligation to make up the fund's deficit.
Even more obvious is the opposition's capacity for condemning and criticizing, without ever suggesting concrete solutions to the problems we are facing in Canada today.
The Leader of the Official Opposition is a case in point. One day he supports free trade and the next he condemns it. One day he supports the GST, the next day he is against it, and the day after he wants to introduce a value added tax. You can never tell what side of the fence he is on.
These people ignore reality and will not face the facts. Above all, they are abysmally ignorant about the taxpayer's ability to pay. And even worse, by spreading false rumours they help create crisis after crisis in this country.

Mr. Speaker, just when the new Clinton administration in the United States is starting to consider ways of controlling escalating drug costs including limits to patent protection, this government pushes ahead with the Senate passage of Bill C-91.
In Bill C-91 the Tory government has complied in advance with the North American free trade agreement.
It has been aided and abetted by the Liberal Party that continues its waffling on free trade.
Last night in the Senate only 30 Liberal senators bothered to show up to vote against Bill C-91. If their full complement of 91 Liberal senators had turned out, this bill would have been defeated.
By their absence the Liberals ensured passage. Liberals once again followed Judy Erola, former Liberal Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and now chief lobbyist for multinational drug companies.
Canadians deserve better representation to protect their rights to affordable health care.

Mr. Speaker, I call upon members of this Parliament to abide by the expectations of our constituents wherein they require that this place be a more respectful place. My constituents have heaped scorn upon all political parties for their behaviour.
As we enter into an election period the tendency will be more and more to achieve recognition by the media and hence our constituents, no matter how silly it may be. Exhibitionist acts that appear to defy authority will likely be tempting some.
This Chamber has seen fish, crows, suggestive gestures, profanity and poor acts of righteous indignation, and I question, impressing whom?
If one is incapable of making one's point through the use of intelligence then surely silence should be considered. In respecting this place perhaps it would be wise to consider respecting those from whom we expect respect.

Mr. Speaker, in September 1988 the Prime Minister announced a $110 million initiative aimed at funding literacy activities over a five-year period. At that time he stated:

February 4, 1993
The time is now long since past when government can sit on the sidelines and leave the issue of illiteracy to the efforts of the voluntary sector.
These programs will come to an end in 1993. So far there is no commitment of government intention to continue funding these literacy programs. As we know, literacy is directly linked to poverty and to unemployment.
The government must act to remove the barrier facing the poor. It must ensure a proper funding policy is in place. The government must recognize that literacy is a right of Canadians and not a privilege.
I call upon the government to do the right thing and continue funding literacy programs in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is Eating Disorders Awareness Week, with the theme "breaking stereotypes, celebrating a healthy weight".
The National Eating Disorders Information Centre and other groups all across Canada will tackle the problem of the obsession with slimness and appearance, especially among women. The purpose is to draw attention to the social factors that contribute to eating disorders, like anorexia, bulimia or obsession with slimness. Information on eating disorders will be given to the public to dispel the myths and indicate where to find the appropriate resources.
I am pleased that the messages being conveyed this week are in keeping with this government's efforts to promote the concept of healthy weight. A healthy body can take many different shapes. Having a healthy weight does not necessarily mean being slim.
I want to congratulate the National Eating Disorders Information Centre for all its efforts to draw attention to this important health problem.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of the families of Sherri-Lee and Maurice Paul and Terri-Lynn Babb, three Manitobans who were murdered in the last month by men whom our justice system could not seem to stop by restraining orders from stalking them and killing them.
I also rise on behalf of Mrs. Sharon Jensen, my constituent, whose daughter Marilyn was killed under similar circumstances last year and who despairs about the political system ever reacting to the work that she has done to try to get this government and the Manitoba government to do something about these crimes. She has fought hard to prevent another mother from going through what she has.
On behalf of these families and all Canadian families whose relatives have been taken by or who live in fear of these kinds of acts, I call upon the Solicitor General to take action now to amend the Criminal Code of Canada to ensure that restraining orders are actually worth more than the paper they are written on, and that we as a society do everything we can to ensure that the system does not fail another family in this way.

Mr. Speaker, one of the most important concerns expressed by Canadians is the need for effective crime prevention in our communities.
In the riding of Elk Island citizens from all walks of life have joined together in organizations such as Rural Crime Watch in an effort to make our homes safer and more secure. As a result of many months of hard work these volunteers have set up a province-wide rural crime watch workshop which will take place this weekend in the community of Nisku.
Participants include representatives from municipal, provincial and federal governments, as well as police, judges, prosecutors and farm organizations. In addition student winners of essay and poster contests will be recognized. The theme of the workshop is working
February 4, 1993

together to prevent crime. Let us all work together for safer communities and a better Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the major concern of people across this country is the unacceptably high unemployment rate and the persistent economic recession.
Despite the government's insistence that good times are just ahead of us, my riding of Northumberland continues to face new job losses, business closures and bankruptcies. Federal government cutbacks to social expenditures and provincial transfer payments have resulted in Northumberland municipalities from Trenton across to Cobourg and Port Hope scrambling to meet new demands on social assistance programs.
Home owners and small businesses are already strangled by numerous federal tax increases. Consequently, our municipalities feel forced to cut necessary services such as day care, dental care, family counselling services, emergency child services and seniors care services.
This government's insistence on dealing with debt through the cutting of programs has increased hardship across this country. People are our nation's most important resource. The government must introduce programs which will encourage wealth creation in this country, introduce people-centred policies and stimulate a sense of hope in a nation with a great future.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot wait.

Mr. Speaker, one of the first and most significant events to take place in my riding in this or any other year was the presentation on January 3 of 101 Governor General's 125th anniversary commemorative medals to citizens of Fredericton-York-Sunbury who have distinguished themselves by their contributions to making Canada a better place in which to live.
These 101 medals were intended to honour not just those citizens selected to receive them, but also to reflect real tribute to the thousands of other men and women who regularly help to build our community and our country. In their own way each of them is truly an unsung hero.
Oral Questions
It is fitting that this medal was commemorating our 125th anniversary and hopefully it will help us to dedicate ourselves to Canada's rich destiny in the 125 years which lie ahead.
I want to express my respect and appreciation to His Excellency, the Governor General, for his wise and sensitive judgment in striking these Canada 125 medals.

["Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Richelieu for his question. As with the previous question, I will certainly pass the hon. member's representations on to the government House leader as soon as possible."]

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Deputy Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister will be meeting with President Clinton tomorrow. President Clinton said he wants new agreements on the environment and on labour conditions to the NAFTA deal before proceeding with NAFTA.
Will the Prime Minister agree with President Clinton tomorrow that he is right in demanding changes to the NAFTA deal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend has got it wrong. President Clinton has said the NAFTA deal will not be changed. He is seeking supplementary agreements to the NAFTA which have nothing to do with the text itself. These have to do with the environment and labour relations.
It also has to do with an arrangement he wants to make with the United States Congress that we have nothing to do with at all. He will ask Congress to increase the amount of labour adjustment policies that they have. That is with good reason because on a per capita basis the Canadian labour adjustment policies such as training and related matters are about two to three times better than those of the United States.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the President of the United States says that he will not proceed with implementing the agreement between the United States, Mexico and Canada until they have obtained satisfaction on the environment and working conditions, it is quite obvious that he wants changes to this agreement.

February 4, 1993
Oral Questions
Since the President of the United States is asking for changes to the agreement, will the Canadian government take advantage of these discussions to ask that Canada obtain the same conditions as Mexico got with respect to energy policies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Tfade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the President has said quite specifically that he is not seeking, repeat not seeking, changes to the agreement. He is seeking some side agreements, what he has called supplementary accords, with Mexico and to an extent with us. He is concerned as much about Mexican cross-border environmental problems as anything else and those will not change the text of the NAFTA agreement.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not understand why the minister is trying to be technical. The President has said the United States will not proceed with NAFTA as long as it is not satisfied that it has the proper conditions concerning the environment and the labour conditions. It is clear that the United States wants some changes.
Will this government take up this occasion to make sure that in the matter of energy Canadians will be treated the same way the Mexicans are being treated by the Americans in that deal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I repeat again, the NAFTA text is not subject to change.
The President has said he is seeking changes with the environment and labour elements that are outside of the text. He is also looking for, as I said a minute ago, changes to the labour adjustment policies in the United States of America. It has nothing to do with Canada.
The fact is that we had been talking about the same type of accord on labour and on the environment with the outgoing administration. We are seeking to continue
those discussions with the incoming administration when they are ready to discuss what the specifics might be.

Mr. Speaker, given recent U.S. trade actions against pork and steel we assume that the Prime Minister in his conversations with the President will seek from him assurances that that sort of trade harassment is now going to end.
Since President Clinton has said that he will seek two parallel or supplementary accords on the environment and on labour standards will the Prime Minister, for his part, now seek a parallel or supplementary agreement on subsidies and anti-dumping which would prevent the sort of harassment we have been seeing in Canada for the past month?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I responded to that question to my hon. friend two days ago.
What we have achieved through the Uruguay round negotiations, which I know he and I both sincerely hope will be completed successfully very soon, is a substantial improvement on the countervailing duty and subsidy arrangements that would affect all countries.
As regards the anti-dumping which is the subject of the steel problems, we and many other countries have tried but there is no willingness on the part of the Americans to change their anti-dumping laws. Their anti-dumping laws are the same as our anti-dumping laws. I am sure my hon. friend is not standing up saying that he wishes to see a reduction or elimination of the protection we have against some actions on the part of American companies hurting Canadian companies.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows in the Uruguay round, the long delayed Uruguay round which we would all welcome, there is provision for a subsidies code.
Will the Prime Minister seek from the President of the United States an assurance that the President will urge an early conclusion of the Uruguay round or if not, that the subsidies code in the Uruguay round be transplanted to NAFTA so we can end this sort of trade harassment we are getting in Canada?
February 4, 1993

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend can be assured absolutely that the Prime Minister will be urging the President to proceed with a satisfactory conclusion of the Uruguay round as soon as possible.
That has been our position for some time now and I will be taking that message to Mr. Kantor when I meet with him. I am sure my hon. friend will be very pleased that will be the position of the Government of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my leader is in Port Hawkesbury visiting the most recent victim of the Canada-U.S. trade deal.
While the Prime Minister said yesterday that the move by Premium Automotive was atypical of Canadian companies, he knows full well as does the Minister for International Trade that since the trade deal was signed over 400,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost in this country. He also knows that the United States administration is harassing Canada on softwood lumber, on steel and on hogs, simply to name a few.
When our Prime Minister visits President Clinton, will he indicate that the Liberal policy of renegotiating the contract is simply not on and that based on the FTA's dismal record Canada will cancel this deal and will not proceed with the North American free trade agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me just quote from an objective analysis of the free trade agreement by the C.D. Howe Research Institute:
"It seems clear that the recession has not been due to factors directly related to the free trade agreement. Indeed, the facts so far are more consistent with the optimistic scenario of free trade supporters than with the views of detractors", like my hon. friend. "Free trade with the United States has helped the development of higher value-added industries that are crucial to Canada's economic growth. In particular, many of Canada's manufacturing sectors seem to have performed remarkably well on the United States market under the free trade agreement".
Oral Questions
If my hon. friend needs any proof of this he need only look to the last Statistics Canada trade results for the first 11 months of last year when our exports to the United States were up 11.9 per cent compared to the year before.
If he goes back to 1988 when the free trade agreement started he will see that Canadian exports are up about double the rate as those from Japan, Germany or the United Kingdom into the United States market. Canadian companies are performing well. They are succeeding under the free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, the minister can say anything he likes but he should recognize that Canadians believe the real way to measure the effectiveness of his policies is by the number of unemployed which continues to escalate in this country.
The minister also knows that again and again we have heard that the Canada-U.S. trade deal was not going to lower our social programs to the lowest common denominator. However, we have an auto parts company in Nova Scotia that may be going to New Hampshire, a U.S. state with no income tax, lax environmental and labour standards and worst of all, an unemployment insurance system just like the one the government is proposing.
Is it a coincidence that this government's Draconian UI reforms conform to states like New Hampshire, or does FTA and NAFTA have something to do with it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the mind boggles when it hears all the inconsistencies riddling the hon. member's question. If he goes right to the heart of the issue he will find that the company in Nova Scotia makes steel gas tanks. Not many companies are using steel gas tanks now. They are using plastic gas tanks. That is the fundamental problem that company has faced. It has not kept up with the marketplace.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the same minister. The minister is always quoting favourable articles with regard to free trade and NAFTA. Can he explain how an American expert has said that the recent U.S. ruling on steel was an example of harassment, corruption and I quote: "reveals the hypocrisy and absurdity of U.S. dumping off"?

February 4, 1993
Oral Questions
While he is on his feet can he also explain how Canadians can get a fair deal in Mexico when IBM officials say they were told to offer a $1 million bribe in order to get a contract that a Canadian company did not get because of the corruption in that country as well?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend and his colleagues in the New Democratic Party do not want to see the NAFTA proceed. They would like to see a country like Mexico kept at low levels of economic performance and low levels of wealth so that it cannot raise its standard of living, its standards of environmental protection, its standards of health care, not through hand-outs from other countries but through its own sources of wealth that will be generated by the free trade agreement.
Surely my hon. friend can take the blindfold off his face and try to look at the positive elements of this agreement on Mexico. Or does he want to see Mexico stay down so that the New Democratic Party can lord themselves over that country?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of health. Yesterday the Tory majority in the Senate rammed through Bill C-91 which effectively harmonizes Canadian drug patent laws with that of the United States. At that very same time in Washington, a Senate committee issued a scathing indictment of U.S. drug patent laws, singling out those laws as the prime reason for escalating U.S. health care costs.
I want to ask the minister of health: Since it is clear that the U.S. Senate says that its system is flawed and since President Clinton of the United States says their system is flawed, why on earth are we adopting the very system that they are about to abandon?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe we had that debate a few weeks ago and we gave the arguments that should be given in terms of intellectual property.
When my friend talks about the health care system in the United States, he knows very well that it is not a question of drugs management. He knows very well that we do not talk about universality in the United States. We know that even if the Americans are not covered, the Canadian system remains exactly the same.
Once again, we had that debate. We showed the evidence that Bill C-91 was good and fortunately the Senate confirmed the decision of the House.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
Arkansas Senator David Pryor, senior adviser to President Clinton, in commenting on this report yesterday said: "Well, what can we do about this situation?" In short, he says that we can shorten the patent life of drug products in the United States. In other words, they could adopt the Canadian system of compulsory licensing, the very system that this government killed last night.
Now that the deed is done, now that the government has killed compulsory licensing, whose interests was this government serving since it is clearly obvious now that it was not the interests of the Canadian public?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer the member by what was said to me yesterday in his own province by a researcher at Dalhousie University. He told me that fortunately Canadian researchers will now be able to keep the property of what has been found in Canada and use it in terms of the way we work. In clinical trials, it will work in terms of the application of that research. It will not go to the United States; it will remain in Canada.
This is exactly why all of the science community is happy with Bill C-91. It represents a big victory for researchers in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
The rantings yesterday of the Prime Minister about the owner of Premium Automotive may make good TV but they do nothing for the unemployed workers who are left out in the cold as a result of his government's incompetence.
February 4, 1993

Oral Questions
Will the Acting Prime Minister instruct the minister for Atlantic development to begin negotiating today with the province of Nova Scotia and with local authorities a plan to create lasting jobs in the Port Hawkesbury area and indeed in the entire strait area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am advised that officials from the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency as well as the province are meeting right now to discuss possible ways of seeking new investors and new ways of keeping that facility open.
My hon. friend and I are of the same mind, that if there is any way that we can keep this facility open and maintain those jobs then that is the objective that we both have.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough. The people in Port Hawkesbury deserve action from this government.
I ask the Acting Prime Minister again: Will he work with the local authorities to create a comprehensive plan to restore the economic health of that area which has been so sadly neglected by his government over the last eight years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, now we have gone from the sublime to the ridiculous. I think my hon. friend must have a very, very short memory. He does not remember that the Cape Breton investment tax credit has been one of the important ways that we have seen jobs created in that part of the country. It has been a very generous tax credit that has generated jobs and has generated opportunities for the people of the country. I think my hon. friend should be reminding his constituents of this because this government has not ignored the plight of those people in his part of the country.

Mr. Speaker, this morning Le Devoir reported that employers have already started to use Bill C-105 to tighten the screws on their employees.
My question is directed to the Minister of State for Employment and Immigration. When will she realize she has just opened the door wide open to employer abuse of employees and when will she withdraw Bill C-105, once and for all?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pauline Browes (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday we had a substantial debate on this issue. Bill C-105 has not come to the floor of the House of Commons for debate to this point.
Let me just remind the member that when we speak of this bill we are looking at whether it is fair that people who are working should be paying for people who choose not to work. Is it fair to restrain the deficit with these measures in terms of people who choose not to work? Is it fair for new workers that come on that employers are able to get those persons without paying UI? Is it fair that more training should be done because of the UI?
I say that this is quite fair.

Mr. Speaker, through you, I want to say to the minister that unemployment insurance is something we all pay for and should not be used as an excuse to impose this burden on the unemployed. It is because of this government's policies that they are being laid off in the first place.
Furthermore, since the beginning of this debate we have heard the government say time and time again that the appeal process will restore the balance. I wish the minister would realize that-
Please put your question.

-the process takes months and even years.

Oral Questions
Again, I want to ask the minister: When will she withdraw the bill? That is the only thing we are waiting for.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pauline Browes (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-105 will come to the floor of the House of Commons with an opportunity to debate. We look to the members of the House of Commons to make any improvements that need to be made at that time.
I want to stress to the people watching today that what this bill is all about is that those people who choose not to work will not get unemployment insurance. There is just cause. There are many reasons why people choose not to work and that would be covered under just cause and those persons would get unemployment insurance. There will be ample opportunity for the discussion of this.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
There is still no resolution to the tragic situation of substance abuse at Davis Inlet. Local people feel that flying children to the United States is not a long-term answer.
I want to ask the minister today to tell the people of Davis Inlet whether he agrees that a treatment program must be culturally based and must be in the Innu language. If he agrees with those principles, will he respond favourably to a request that will come forward from Davis Inlet today or tomorrow based on those lines?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, what I announced yesterday was an immediate answer to an emergency problem with the kids who were involved last week in the gas sniffing problem. Obviously we are waiting for the community. As I said yesterday, no decision will be made which would be contrary to what the community wants to do.
I heard the vice-chief say this morning that they would prefer to have a treatment centre within-not the reserve because they are not reserve Indians-their community.
I do not turn down that proposal. However, tomorrow morning we have people from the federal level and the provincial level who will discuss with people in Davis Inlet. They will certainly come up with a proposal. If the nature of the proposal is the same one that my friend proposes, I will certainly consider that option.

Mr. Speaker, there is a location called Border Beacon just west of Davis Inlet which has an airstrip and facilities and which could be put in place at relatively little cost.
That I believe is the preferred option of the local people. I want to ask the minister whether he believes that is the best option with a holistic approach to treatment. When that proposal for a Border Beacon treatment centre comes forward, will he see that the finances are put in place immediately to fund such a treatment centre?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my officials have been instructed to discuss that option with the people tomorrow.
However, I want to raise in the House the question of gas sniffing and the problem of suicide, particularly within the aboriginal community. In December I met with the chiefs from different provinces. I will again meet with them in March. The problem is one of the major mental health problems we have with aboriginal people in Canada.
The decision we make for Davis Inlet is very important for those people. We have to keep in mind that the problem goes beyond the people we are talking about. We have to consider all the communities we deal with across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the acting minister of immigration.
February 4, 1993

Earlier this week, there were serious charges from members of the Immigration and Refugee Board in Montreal that they were pressured by senior officials to make decisions on refugee applications contrary to the facts. This is a repetition of similar incidents in Toronto last year.
Considering that the Immigration and Refugee Board is supposed to be an independent tribunal, will the government initiate an independent public inquiry into these serious charges and take steps to stop these incidents immediately?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pauline Browes (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the comments that the hon. member makes are serious. I would expect that he would be providing details himself of where there are incidents of some wrongdoing.
The Immigration Appeal Board and the Immigration and Refugee Board are independent bodies. They make decisions weighing the facts of the matter. If there is some specific information that the member wishes to share with the department or with me, I would be pleased to review it.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has not answered the question.

Last November, Dr. Sam Ifejika resigned from the board in Toronto, alleging that board members were under political pressure. There were also instances of racist remarks, ridicule and mismanagement.
When will the government start cleaning up this very important board and stop its appointments of incompetent political friends?

When will the government take these matters seriously?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pauline Browes (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you know that each of the members who are appointed to boards and commissions have the opportunity to be reviewed by standing committees.
I would say there are very few members who have been appointed to such commissions that members of the opposition have taken the opportunity to review. It has been the position of the government that there is an opportunity to review the qualifications of Immigration
Oral Questions
and Refugee Board members. You will find that the qualifications of those persons who have been appointed by Orders in Council to independent bodies have been excellent appointments. Indeed, we are very proud that so many women have been appointed to those boards as well as representatives of visible minorities in order to have proper representation of the Canadian population.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. First, I want to congratulate him on his new post. I see members scurrying about in their seats over there. That is how you get action in the House, Mr. Speaker.
Many of us, including the minister, were in Saskatoon last week for the rally of some 13,000 Saskatchewan farmers. The minister's own department says that Saskatchewan farm income last year was at the lowest level in constant dollars since 1938. I wonder if the minister can tell us whether he is ready to make an announcement on a third line of defence, an emergency payout to western farmers which would help not only the farmers but people in jobs in small towns, villages and cities across the prairies.
As a new minister is he willing to look at a new farm policy where farmers are paid a price based on the cost of production with a cap of 7,000 or 8,000 bushels of wheat? This would help the small farmer more than the large farmer. I am asking about the emergency pay out and a new farm program.

Mr. Speaker, what the hon. member did not point out was that the members who were scurrying around were from his side, rushing back to sit behind him so it would look like he had some support for what he was saying.
The member raises a serious question. No doubt there is concern in the farm community, especially on the grain and oilseeds side of agriculture, as Saskatchewan is the biggest producer of these commodities in the country.
If you look at the programs that the federal government has put in place, the majority of the money that has gone into special programs has gone into the province of Saskatchewan. He might be interested in knowing that the anticipation is that close to a billion dollars will be paid out in farm programs in this calendar year in the province of Saskatchewan.

Oral Questions
It is not all bad news. Cattle prices are very strong. We had a larger than anticipated final payment go out from the Canadian Wheat Board at the beginning of the year. We will be monitoring the situation. We are always willing to look at new programs. What he is suggesting is that we adopt the NDP farm policy. We are not prepared to do that, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the same minister or the Minister for International Trade.
We heard the minister indicate there is no longer much interest from the government in maintaining its third line of defence policy which has been part of the agricultural promise for the last couple of years.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-98, an act to provide additional borrowing authority for the fiscal year beginning on April 1, 1992, be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I was going over some of the things we have done as government in terms of the fundamentals. I suggested that we have those well in place and positioned to do very well as the economy continues to grow.
I mentioned interest rates. Interest rates are the lowest they have been in 20 years, as is inflation and our productivity has grown remarkably in the last couple of years. In terms of the fundamentals we are in a position that our economy can grow. It has been suggested by the G-7 nations that of all the G-7 nations, and most economic think-tanks including many Canadian think-tanks are telling us that in 1993 Canada will lead the rest of the world in growth. It is simply because of the fundamentals we have in place that will allow our Canadian economy to grow.
February 4, 1993

Today we are debating a borrowing bill. We are talking of borrowing somewhere in the vicinity of $8 billion in borrowing authority. Those on the other side of the House are appalled by the fact that the Government of Canada has to borrow $8 billion. That is about the only thing we agree on, because none of us can take a whole lot of pleasure in knowing that the Government of Canada has to borrow money to keep going.
That is where our agreement ends because since I have been in this House, the other side has never offered any suggestions that would eliminate the need to borrow. That is what we want to do. We do not want to borrow money, but the reality is we are in the position that we have to. In fact, if the spending habits of the Liberals when they were in power had continued when we took office, we would not be talking about borrowing $8 billion today. We would be talking about borrowing $16 billion to just compare our numbers with theirs.
In other words, the amount of accumulated Canadian debt today would not be in the order of $400 billion. It would be pushing close to $900 billion, in fact close to $1 trillion if we had continued in the same line the Liberals practised during their regime back in the late 1970s leading into the early 1980s right up until the time we took office in 1984.
None of those individuals on the other side of the House have ever supported any of our measures in attempting to trim or reduce the size and spending of government. They are talking out of both sides of their mouths on this issue.
What comes to mind are some of the positions the leader of the Liberal Party has taken in the last number of weeks. I would like to read the entire editorial in today's The Ottawa Sun. It is entitled "Vanishing act". I think it very well sums up the position of the Liberal Party under its leader:
Jean Chretien has come up with his own Liberal brand of voodoo economics by promising taxpayers that a future Liberal government would simply wave a magic wand and make the nasty old GST disappear.
Trouble is, when you see through the smoke and mirrors you discover the Liberals would actually replace the unpopular tax with a brand new business transfer tax of their own.
Government Orders
In this article he calls it a sort of Grit sneaky tax. He says:
Make no mistake: This scam is little more than a hidden tax intended to fool taxpayers.
Under the plan, businesses would be required to total their sales, subtract their costs, and then pay a percentage back to the government.
The poor consumers would still have to pay higher prices, of course. They just wouldn't see it spelled out in bold print on their receipts at the checkout counter in the form of a 7% tax.
It goes on to say:
Taxpayers aren't about to be tricked by the sleight of hand, not when their money rides on the cards.
If Chretien is to replace the GST, he must find a credible way to raise the $15 billion in lost revenue.
But if a hidden business transfer tax is his idea of tax reform, then Chretien had better do his homework before hitting the hustings.
Taxpayers' memories aren't that short. They remember the GST was intentionally not buried into the price of goods and services so as to stop future governments like his from hiking it every time they need a fresh injection of cash.
That was the one modest concession taxpayers received-an assurance that no future government of any political stripe could raise the tax without immediate hell to pay from the taxpayers.
In conclusion, it says:
Putting the tax out of sight won't put it out of mind for voters, no matter what Chretien thinks.
For that reason he should think again.
Getting back again to the point which I am attempting to make, we do have a huge debt problem in this country. It is not going to go away by simply waving a magic wand. The Canadian people know that, the Liberal leader does not. If he is talking about eliminating the GST, he is fooling no one but himself.
There are only three basic ways for governments to tax. It can tax income, it can tax capital and it can tax consumption. If one of those areas is eliminated, which the leader of the Liberal Party is suggesting, the consumption tax, there are only two other areas in which he can tax. That is what he has to grapple with and that is why I am suggesting the Canadian people will understand when it comes time to vote. They do not want any more smoke and mirrors, they want the truth. The truth is the Government of Canada cannot forgo $15 billion in tax.

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
That is not the only thing the Liberals have said in regard to the tax over the last number of years. Originally they condemned us for having to deal with the idea of taxation. I guess they believed that if we did go ahead with that tax and if we did bring in a new GST that our political life would be threatened. They could march into office without having to say anything and without having to show their hand. That is exactly what they are doing.
A $400 billion debt is a problem for any government. It is a problem for ours. I am suggesting that if we had followed the course laid out and that is being laid out now by the Liberal Party, that debt today would have doubled and we would really be behind the eight ball.
There are many ways to measure debt. The way I would like to measure it today would be the measure of debt that we have in this country in relation to the goods and services produced in this country. In other words let us measure our debt against our gross domestic product and find out where we stand.
In 1984 when we took office, the debt or deficit when measured against the goods and services produced in this country was in the area of 9 per cent. In the last eight years, we have reduced it to the level of 4.5 per cent.
We are on the right track. It is going to be a long and painful recovery but we are not going to achieve results by attempting to fool the Canadian people and in a sense, fooling ourselves.
We will continue to attack the problem and we will continue to take the political heat for having done it. At the end of the day, the Canadian people are going to figure it out. They are going to tell us that we on this side of the House have done what was necessary. It was not popular but it was necessary.
I am going to leave it at that. I know that we have 10 minutes of questions and answers. I will be pleased to answer any questions from the other side of the House.
