Mr. Speaker, I know the previous speaker is very sincere in what he
says. We believe that it is the wrong and inappropriate course to take. We will continue to attack. I suggest that they are attacking the wrong things. The Canadian public acknowledges the fact that the attack is on the wrong places.
His demeanour is a little bit better than the tenor of the debate this morning. It got a little bit rancorous when a pre-election type of mood was prevalent in the Chamber. This morning one hon. member indicated to the hon. member from Brampton that he was stupid. That is totally inappropriate. There is no place for that in debate. It continued to get worse and worse and really debased the House. At least I acknowledge that the hon. member is sincere in what he says even though he is probably totally incorrect.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: And misguided.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I should add totally misguided. This is the borrowing authority where the government wishes the authority to borrow another $8 billion to expend in areas which it should not. Its priorities are totally misguided. We are talking big bucks here. Yet to bring it into total perspective, I was totally shocked that the Minister of Labour, in response to a letter from a constituent, came to tell me that the federal minimum wage is $4 an hour. Very few people know that. I could not believe it at first. I am incredulous that the federal minimum wage is $4 an hour.
In Newfoundland, the minimum wage is $4.75; in P.E.I. it is $4.75; in Ontario, not surprisingly it is $6.35. However the federal government's minimum wage is $4 per hour. The minister says he is going to take a look at it.
We are talking about borrowing millions of dollars and we cannot afford to raise the wages of those very few people who earn as little as $4 an hour. The government should give a late Christmas present to these people and give them an instant raise to about $6 an hour. We are looking to borrow millions of dollars and we cannot afford to give a person who is making $4 an hour any kind of increase. The last increase was from $3.50 to $4 in 1986. We are talking about priorities. That is the kind of misguided priority this government has.
February 4, 1993

We talk about deficit. We have a certain amount of sympathy for deficit reduction, but at the same time on whose back does the deficit reduction have to fall?
I know that Ontario has been hardest hit by the recession. Seventy-nine per cent of all job losses have been to Ontario; 54 per cent of the increase in unemployment is in Ontario; 37 per cent of Canada's population is in Ontario; 39 per cent of total bankruptcies are in Ontario. The federal government has continued to pass the buck but not the bucks. They have passed the buck to the province and the province in turn, without choice, has to pass the buck to the municipalities.
The latest initiative by the federal government, which has not come forward yet because there are discussions, are the grants in lieu of taxes. Federal buildings and properties in municipalities across this country are not taxed. The federal government will pay a grant instead of taxes. It may very well be appropriate.
However, right now the government is saying it might have to cut back on the grants to the municipalities. As a result, the buck will again be passed to the municipalities. This time the province is bypassed. The municipalities will have to increase the tax base within the municipality and the local politicians will have to take the heat for that. Once again the federal government chooses to pass on the responsibility. It is letting someone else take the heat of its actions.
I suppose there is a ray of hope. Government members say the recession is over, and I would be very happy if I completely believed it. One gentleman on Bank Street at the Camera Exchange has been in that location for 12 or so years. I do not think he would be concerned that I am mentioning the name of the business. He has a big sign saying: "I am sorry, I did not know the recession was over but I am now bankrupt". Many Canadians can relate to that.
Statistics Canada says the recession is over, but certainly we have no indication that it is. Statistics may say one thing, but reality says something else. There are a number of bankruptcies at present and the number continues to escalate. The number of unemployed remains at 11.8 per cent. In my community it is about 16 or 17 per cent. I suggest in some communities it is probably
Government Orders
a lot higher than that. There is always somebody worse off than you.
I want to go back to priorities. The government continually looks for villains. It says to the unemployed that if you quit your job or leave it under circumstances which it does not approve, then it is going to have to cut your unemployment insurance. The villain in this case is made out to be the people who leave their jobs for one reason or another, but no one in this government ever talks about those other villains. Perhaps the terminology is inappropriate. Erase the word villains. Other individuals who could be responsible for part of this deficit that we have accumulated, all of us.
No one in this government has yet responded in any sensible way at least about the family trusts. The wealthiest families in this country are able to set aside millions and millions of dollars for their children. The previous government said it was going to give them 25 years and they could pay taxes on those millions and millions and millions of dollars in 21 years.
This government said that 21 years was not long enough to get their finances in order, so it is going to wait until the last child of that family passes away. They may need another 21 years. If you are a multimillionaire you may have 35 years to get your finances in order.
What happens when a constituent calls my office and says that Revenue Canada is breathing down his neck? Let us say he owes $1,200 and he cannot pay it. Revenue Canada is calling his place of employment saying if he does not pay soon he will be in trouble. That is the problem. We are not pointing to the people we should. Come on, get involved with the deficit reduction. We do not hear from this side.
Certainly not one of our big fans is Diane Francis who has written a book called Controlling Interest. I recommend this reading for the Conservative members who are here and those who are not here. It talks about the wealthiest families in this country. Canada has one of the greatest concentrations of wealth in the whole world. She says that fewer and fewer people are controlling more and more of the country's finances and if we do not force them to pay any income tax, they will continue to get richer and richer.

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
They are the paper entrepreneurs. There is not even any money exchanged, it is just paper, but they get wealthier and wealthier. This government says it does not want to tax them at this time. It wants to give them a little while longer.
One of the reasons the government gave was they may have a disabled child and want to provide for their future. If you are a multimillionaire and you have a disabled child, I would hope that you would care for that child. To say that you have to pass this legislation to protect this child is just not acceptable. It is incredulous. You would perhaps put a small little adjunct to a piece of legislation to say okay, if there is a disabled child in the family, allow them to do this but not to exempt everybody.
I would recommend this book. This is good reading because Diane Francis is a big supporter of these folks, a great friend, but in this she says something is dramatically wrong.
The government continually says we have got to have our fundamentals. The Prime Minister says every day we have to get our fundamentals right before we move forward. I keep repeating that after eight years of just about anything, if you do not have the fundamentals right you have obviously failed. It is obviously time to change direction. You have to get beyond the fundamentals.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Falling flat on them.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Falling flat on your fundamentals.
I was a teacher for 28 years. If I could not teach the fundamentals to somebody in eight years, I would have been on my head. You are an absolute failure as a teacher. Therefore you are an absolute failure as a government. You cannot blame the student and you cannot blame the residents of this country for your failures. Please get off that fundamental kick. You had better change the fundamentals.
I want to talk about Hibernia for a few moments. Hibernia is a massive project, $5.2 billion. We support the project but Canadians are saying we want our fair share of the contracts. The government is a shareholder and an investor. Last year Algoma Steel lost a contract
to a Belgian steel company. I went to St. John's. Believe me, they were very hospitable. I think they had very good explanations at that time, but we were convinced that Belgium was dumping steel in Canada.
This past week MIL Davie of Quebec said it was not even allowed to bid on a contract for steel. It went to South Korea. It was not even allowed to bid.
The minister is up on this. He said yesterday that there are steel companies that are going to benefit from a rebar contract next week. I have been told on many occasions that if any other country had a megaproject of that size, there would be an absolute guarantee, not a target, a guarantee that there would be jobs created in that country because of such a project.
Trade deals? Obviously miserable failures. We are losing our manufacturing base. In 1990, of the jobs created in Canada, I believe 91 per cent were service oriented. I have nothing against service oriented jobs, but you cannot base a country's future strictly on service oriented jobs.
I am going to recommend more reading: The Work of Nations by Robert Reich who is perhaps the main architect of President Clinton's new economic policies in the United States. He is an individual with a very refreshing sense of a new direction for the country. I listened in on his confirmation hearings. He talked about labour law. He said he was going to introduce anti-scab legislation and there was not a whimper, not a whimper from Republican congressmen.
Yet the Ontario government talked about that and, lo and behold, we thought for sure the sky would fall and every business would leave Ontario, we could be assured of it. Surely, Mr. Speaker, you see the irony of this.
In The Work of Nations Mr. Reich talks about why the rich get richer and the poor get poorer. In the United States he said fewer and fewer people are in control of more and more money. That left the poorest fifth of Americans by 1990 with 3 per cent of the nation's total income, down from 5.5 per cent 20 years earlier. It is called the old trickle down economics. If we just leave it to the market to decide, it will indeed decide. It will decide to keep it to the upper level of the country, not to the bottom group. We have to learn to be more equitable in everything we do in this country.
February 4, 1993

The GST is the most hated tax ever brought about by any government. I did a survey of all the businesses in my community. I thought businesses were big supporters of the government. No. They said: "Scrap it. Scrap the GST because we cannot afford it, it is an administrative nightmare. Everybody who buys something from me says I am at fault for this." It has created more underground trade than ever before. It just was the wrong tax at the wrong time. It is a hated tax. Every single day and with every single purchase people are reminded. They have a genuine distaste.
Of course the government is going to say: "It is a lot of money. We make a lot of money out of the GST. What are you going to do? How are you going to get it?"
Neil Brookes of Osgoode Hall, a renowned economist, has identified a series of tax breaks that cost the Canadian treasury more than $8 billion a year and primarily benefits business and the rich. He said that we could scrap them without harming the economy. Rather than demanding lower taxes, Canadians should be demanding fairer taxes and a better social welfare system.
Again, if people are on any government assistance they are painted as being a freeloader, they do not want to work, they have no ambition and we should not be paying them what they are receiving. I say in many other countries in this world, in countries which have economies that are doing quite well, they do not point out these people as being free loaders. They say it is just fine. It is an acceptance and I give them credit. However, through a continual barrage of negativism we bring the load from those up here to those down here. It is misplaced, misguided, unfortunate and inappropriate. One would wish that we would stop on that kind of bent.
Municipal infrastructure I know has been a random shot. Let us get on with it. I think everybody but the government says: "Let's go for it". Sixty-three thousand jobs created almost instantly. It says it is going to cost us too much. It is going to cost us $400 million in the deficit over a five-year period. That is not too much.
I could see the psychological lift. People have given up hope. They say that if they get the fundamentals right any longer we will all be gone. There will not be a country, there will not be an economy left. For God's sake, do something. This is one thing that is a very
Government Orders
positive step. Everybody is ready to go ahead. They have all the engineering. Every municipality is saying they have problems but they are prepared to get involved. The provinces are prepared to get involved.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this bill.
I want to begin by referring to some remarks that government members said repeatedly during their speeches today. I refer specifically to the member for Carleton-Charlotte and the member for Brampton who kept saying that the government is creating a climate where jobs can be created. They kept repeating that phrase "creating a climate where jobs can be created". The other sentence they repeatedly used was: "We are making sure the fundamentals are right; we are putting the fundamentals in place".
I say to the government that inflation, and I cannot debate this point with them, is under control. I give the government credit for that. I have said before in this House that I think its ratchet on inflation is too aggressive. I think that the expense in terms of the number of people who are unemployed is too severe. Having said that, I acknowledge that the almost zero inflation in this country is something that the government should get recognition for. I would also say that because of that we have lower interest rates. That is as far as I go with this government.
I happen to believe that the fundamental issue that the government has ignored has been the tax system of this country. This government came to power in 1984 with a very strong commitment to comprehensive personal and corporate tax reform. Here we are nine years later and we still have probably the most complicated, most complex tax act in the world.
Even the best tax lawyers and tax accountants in this country will readily admit that this tax act is an unmitigated disaster. The rules, regulations, exceptions and the exceptions to exceptions make it an instrument that only very few can use.
I believe, and I have believed this for three years, that this tax act is one of the most fundamental reasons why there is absolutely no trust and no confidence or spirit or very little spirit or confidence left in this country.

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
A tax act should be considered something that is good. The tax act is mostly built on trust and has to meet certain tests. It must be fair, it must be simple and it must be efficient. This tax act does not meet any one of those tests.
In fact, last year 80 per cent of the tax returns filed in this country had mistakes in them and they had to be returned to be corrected. What a waste of money. What an inefficient instrument. The only people who really know how to use this instrument are the corporations whose wealth, sales, profits and retained earnings are so large that they can afford expensive tax lawyers and tax accountants.
A senior official of one corporation in this countiy whose sales are in the billions of dollars told me: "I have 40 tax lawyers working for me. With this tax act I have orchestrated a situation so that I have not had to pay tax in 10 years". It is all legal. There is nothing illegal. It is just this 20-year document from budget after budget, Liberal and Conservative budgets. I am not saying that we have not played a part in building up this complex and archaic instrument. The bottom line is that this tax act has now broken the trust we have with average Canadians.
That is the reason that for the last three years I have been trying to advance debate with a constructive alternative to this tax act. The idea I have been proposing is the single tax system. This is not an idea that I created. It is an idea that has been debated for 15 or 20 years. Some would argue that the idea goes back 40 or 50 years.
My initial source of information on this idea came from respected economists at Stanford University, Dr. Robert Hall and Dr. Alvin Rabushka. They are Americans but the same basic principle applies here. In their presentation of the single tax system they basically argue that because the tax act has reached such a level of unfairness, complexity and inefficiency we must get back to basics. We must stop running the economy of the country through the tax act. We should go back to using the tax act as an instrument just for collecting revenue for the treasury, for collecting the amount we need to ensure that our health care system and our social security systems are all looked after.
The tax act should not be used for other economic instruments. In other words we should flush out all the loopholes, flush out all the corporation loopholes and all those exceptions and those exceptions to exceptions. If a particular corporation needs money from the Government of Canada, regardless of whether it is in the energy sector, the forestry sector or a manufacturing sector, let it come to the respective department of government and put forward its case. Make the corporation justify it in terms of job creation and let the line department grant it the money, whether through an interest free loan or a grant, and link it to job creation. Let the political fathers decide whether that taxpayers' money should go out.
Right now, we have a tax act under which between $30 billion and $40 billion worth of grants are going to business with absolutely no accountability. There are corporations in this countiy that are using tax preferences, some of them 15 years old. They were given it for a policy objective that was maybe relevant 15 years ago but is no longer relevant today. It is buried in the act and so they get that tax preference. It is nothing more than a grant to corporations.
We on this side of the House talk about examining alternatives to the GST, and my leader has stated unequivocally that we are going to scrap the GST. We are going to scrap the GST because the GST was a very poorly designed tax implemented at a very bad time. The concept of a consumption tax is not a bad idea but this government has designed the tax so poorly that it has really been the straw that has broken the camel's back, in terms of the spirit or the attitude of Canadians toward tax policy in this country. Nothing less than the scrapping of the GST will be acceptable to Canadians. Make no mistake about it, my leader is not fudging on this particular commitment. He is not fudging. It is not going to be a maybe yes and a maybe no. The GST is going to be scrapped.
The government is always asking, as are journalists and other so-called experts, where we are going to get the $15 billion to replace it. There are many areas in which we can pick up $15 billion.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Name a few.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I am going to name many right now. First, as a result of the current unfairness, inefficiency and complexity of this tax act, which this government supports, we right now have an underground economy in this country second to Italy. It is over $100 billion. If
February 4, 1993

members do not believe me then they should phone Professor W. E. Diewert at the University of British Columbia. He has spent the last 10 years of his life studying the underground economy in Canada. If we have a fair, simple and efficient tax system in this country some of that underground economy will come back on stream. That is one source of funds.
Second, I support the NDP 1,000 per cent with respect to trust funds. There are guestimates that there are anywhere from $20 billion to $50 billion in those trust funds. I actually know some people who have those trust funds and quite frankly I do not think some of them would mind. That law was an Edgar Benson law, it was a Liberal law made 21 years ago. Do not nail me today for something we did 21 years ago. We must change that trust law. There is probably $2 billion or $3 billion that we could take out of those trust funds without affecting those people in any way, shape or form. That is the second area from which we can get some revenue.
Third, last year taxpayers paid about $69 billion in personal income tax. Corporations paid about $11 billion to the treasury, and of that figure $8 billion was paid by small business. Only about $2.5 billion came from large business, mostly foreign multinationals. I cannot believe there is not a member on that side of the House who does not believe that we can find some tax preferences hidden in that $40 billion which we could redirect and redistribute without losing a single corporation.
Ultimately it is not corporations that pay tax but people who pay tax. The trade minister's point is that we must increase productivity. If we treat people fairly productivity will go up because people will make better products at better prices. That is where our exports come in and that is how we are going to reduce our current account deficit.
The only instrument this House of Commons has left with which to mobilize the will of this country, the only instrument this country has left with which to galvanize Canadians and to show Canadians that we are going to treat them fairly is the tax act. We do not need a pro-business tax policy but a pro-people tax policy. That is where the single tax comes in.
Are those enough examples of where we could get the $15 billion? I will just repeat them.
Government Orders
I want to repeat my examples of possible sources of the the $15 billion: One, the underground economy; two, the trust funds; three, let us look at the tax preferences; and four, efficiency and increased productivity because people feel they are being treated fairly.
I have had members on this side of the House and people on the street ask: "How come your party and your leader do not endorse the single tax?" My leader has said repeatedly that he is looking at the single tax idea as one of the options. However, I cannot stand up here today and say that the single tax is perfect because I do not have access to all the books and records on that side of the House. However, it is a doable instrument. It is something that can be done but we need political will to do it.
I am not even saying that the single tax is perfect but it is a viable instrument that allows us to advance debate. Canadians are no longer going to accept the status quo. The status quo is gone. I predict that if this Minister of Finance-and I happen to like this Minister of Finance, I like his style and his attitude and everything about him so this is nothing personal-brings in a budget with anything less than a pro-people tax policy then I guarantee that he is history.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to congratulate my hon. friend on the work he has done on the single tax, and particularly for coining the phrase single tax. This is a very important contribution to work in this area.
Although he may find it difficult to believe that members on this side may occasionally agree with things said by the other side, it is very important that we develop some kind of simple, visible, fair rate of tax, and particularly a system which is not a flat tax.
He may have noticed in The Ottawa Sun of February 4, there is a particularly ridiculous article saying that a flat tax is wrong, and it goes on to talk about work that he and I have been doing from time to time, completely misrepresenting it. It is an article by Rick Gibbons of The Ottawa Sun. I wonder if he could explain to us how his concept of the single tax would be a progressive or gradual tax.

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
In my own studies I have found that the principle of having an income support system connected with the single rate of tax and integrating those two is a veiy succinct and straightforward way of having a progressive tax system that takes people from the income support or welfare system right through to the highest incomes in a very fair and visible way. I wonder if he could tell us how his concept deals with progressivity.
I think there is a lot of misunderstanding about a single tax or a single tax system being simplistic. In fact many people say that things like RRSPs, the Canada Pension Plan, charities and child care, all of the things that we need to consider in a tax system, are not properly considered in these systems. I wonder if he could give us his ideas on those aspects as well.
I believe that is all I have to say, but I would like to again congratulate him for the work he has done in bringing the Hall-Rabushka ideas very much into the Canadian context.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is tough to accept a compliment from the government. I had better be careful.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Go ahead, take a bow.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I want to begin by saying that we have shared ideas on many occasions and we are committed to comprehensive reform. I thank the member again for his support and encouragement.
I want to first of all react to the article by Mr. Gibbons in The Ottawa Sun. A year ago the Sun organization and The Financial Post were the only two papers in Canada that substantially endorsed the work on the single tax. Maybe the Sun organization has switched its position.
For starters, he should not be calling it a flat tax so we are not even talking about the same thing. The single rate of tax is a concept which basically says that we are going to throw away all of the massive numbers of tax preferences that are in the act, but not without being sensitive to the notion of progressivity.
In the single tax that I have designed, and there is room for debate on this, there are progressive features for making sure there are very generous credits for senior citizens, families with children, charitable donations. We have not disturbed the RRSP structure. On the corporate side, we had a very progressive feature by
making sure that the first $100,000 on the corporate side is a tax credit, which is extremely beneficial for small business in this country.
The original idea of a flat tax did not have any of those progressive features built into it. I have not read the article by Mr. Gibbons so I really should not comment.
Let us go to the hon. member's point. I know he is ahead of me on the notion of linking it to an income support system, which I totally support. I must confess that I have not figured out how to do it. Can he imagine if we could have an income support system which would do away with all the duplication and all the bureaucracies in all the provinces across this country.
I think we could win respect overnight if we ever did something like that. Once again the political will for this kind of reform is now the government's challenge. If it does not do it, then it will be ours.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by congratulating my friend and colleague from Broadview-Greenwood, not only on his remarks in the last few minutes in this Chamber, but equally on the persistence he has shown on the single tax idea or more generally on the need to simplify, not make less effective, but make more understandable our tax system. I want to congratulate him and encourage him to keep up the work.
I have done my part rather publicly in spreading the gospel and taking his very excellent pamphlet on the single tax and distributing it to a number of people, to school groups and other groups that have a particular interest in this subject, including some groups that can promote the idea. I say to him, hang in there. It is a question of time.
We have before us another bill looking for more money. Can you think, Mr. Speaker, of any crowd that more deserves yet another licence to print money than the group which sits opposite as the government? It wants to borrow more money. I will come back to that.
Let me share a thought with you, Mr. Speaker. I suppose I do not have the right to have any real contempt for anybody or any group of people, so perhaps the word I am looking for is pity. If I do not have contempt, I at least have pity for a couple of groups of people in society.
February 4, 1993

My friend from St. John's East can rest easy. He is neither one of the individuals I am thinking about nor is he in any of the groups I am thinking about.
If I were capable of real downright contempt it would be for a couple of groups of people: those who trigger false fire alarms and those who make obscene phone calls. Both come from a discipline of cowardice, of meanness, not to mention that they inflict some pretty unfair cost on society when they pull that false fire alarm. They trigger a whole sequence of events, all of which cost money and in some cases a fair amount of anguish. Of course the obscene phone call is in a class by itself with respect to the human cost, the anguish that it causes.
Mr. Speaker, being the astute gentleman that you are, you are sitting there saying: "What does this have to do with Bill C-98, the borrowing bill". I do not want to suggest that anybody on the opposite side is either of the ilk that would make obscene phone calls or trigger false fire alarms. That is not my point. I wanted to get the attention of the House to a couple of the characteristics, rather disreputable characteristics, despicable characteristics involved in those two activities, the attribute of unfairness of inflicting undue cost, the characteristic of cowardice.
I want to put before the House a couple of very specific examples that have a lot to do with this borrowing bill. For example, take the matter we have just dealt with and will continue to deal with in this House, the unemployment insurance changes.
In particular, take the government's proposal that henceforth people who quit their jobs will forfeit their eligibility for unemployment insurance. I know the fine print and I know the nice words that accompany it. I will do the government a favour and I will mention those words too. It says if they quit without just cause. That is fair if it is stopped right there but that is not the signal it sends out.
We come back to the other two activities I mentioned. It comes back to the question of being unfair and mean. The government's intention to do that sends a far larger signal. If it wants to catch the work interloper, the person who only works when he or she has to in order to get a few bucks or a few stamps, if that is who it wants to catch, there is a way to do that. The government does not
Government Orders
have to use a sledge-hammer. It does not have to cause a lot of anguish. It does not have to set up circumstances whereby people will be obliged to stay in occupations despite harassment.
I could set up examples where people whose basic instinct is to work have been put in situations where despite their best efforts, the relationship in the work place has been such, either from the standpoint of personal harassment or sexual harassment, that it has become untenable to work in that place.
Under the bill they have the option of quitting because as the rhetoric on the other side says: Well, it is only a matter of time and they can prove they had just cause. But in the interim, who buys the groceries during that month or that year when they are proving just cause?
I could equally talk about the category of people who get fired and the provisions for them under that bill. Again, without going into detail, that goes straight to the issue of cowardice on the part of the government. It puts the employers in the driver's seat and it lets the employee fend for himself or herself. It is cowardly and it is mean.
Let me give another example. I was talking with my friend, the minister of fisheries, only yesterday about this issue. We had an exchange here in the House during Question Period on Wednesday. I raised with him the circumstances involving people who have lost their groundfish licences because of a very arbitrary, a very cowardly, a very costly and a very mean stipulation about inactive licences.
As I have said to the minister privately, in a letter and in the House yesterday, I basically understand where he is coming from. He is again using a sledge-hammer. If the licence is inactive-emphasis is on the word inactive. If it is inactive groundfish licences he is talking about, these people who live in the Gaspe, the Magdalen Islands in Quebec, New Brunswick, P.E.I., Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, those thousands of people altogether totalling 2,800 to 3,000 people who will be directly deprived of their licences if this measure goes through unchanged.
What does the minister mean by inactive licences? He has defined it as if they have had no catches during the past two years, 1991 and 1992, then the licences are inactive. Well, are they?

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
Perhaps a couple of other circumstances apply. Perhaps there were people like those living in the Rose Blanche area or Isle aux Morts who have had a winter fishery for many years, dozens of years. During the last five years, starting in 1988 through to this year, they have found that their landings have dropped off. In the case of the community of Rose Blanche it is from four million pounds in a three month fishery down to 100,000 pounds.
Some of them in their wisdom and looking after their own pocket-books came to the conclusion it was not worth spending $50 on gas and food to go out and catch $20 worth of fish so they did not go. They kept in touch with a neighbour or two in the community who went out. They found out Joe did not get any fish yesterday or the day before so there was not much point in their spending the money on gas and food to go out and go further in the hole, or as the song says "another day older and deeper in debt".
So they did the prudent thing from the standpoint of their family budget. They stayed ashore. Why? Because they were lazy? No, because they were smart. They were smart enough to figure out that if you spend $50 to make $20 you are even further in the hole than you were before you went out that morning. So many of them elected to stay home, not to stay home because they were lazy, but to stay away from fishing.
They had no landings for those two years. Some of them because they had some initiative went a step further and said: "Since I cannot go fishing, since it does not make sense to spend $50 to make $20, maybe in the meantime I will look around for a job driving nails, painting buildings, working ashore for a few months". Does that mean they had abandoned the fishery? Not quite. The fishery had somewhat abandoned them at least temporarily, or the fish had abandoned them. So they went off and got other seasonal jobs and they had no landings during those two years.
Now had the minister said before the fact that if they did not have landings over a certain period of time then he would consider the licence to be inactive, that is a matter of fairness. However, to write the rules after the fact is very cowardly and unfair.
Mr. Speaker, if you think that is a graphic example let me give you a really graphic one. I spoke in the last 24
hours by phone to a gentleman in my riding in the community of Petites. Now Petites is an isolated community. You cannot reach it by road. It is literally a 15-minute boat ride from the community of Rose Blanche, Harbour le Cou which my hon. friend from St. John's East will know very well.
For the last 12 or 13 years this gentleman in Petites, every morning save maybe Sunday, but five or six days a week has gotten out of his bed at three o'clock or four o'clock in the morning and has taken the 15-minute trip over to Rose Blanche to join a boat crew of four other people. A total of five people. They have fished together for a number of years.
Now keep in mind that my friend from Petites is not the skipper of that boat but is one of five members who crew that boat. There is the skipper, my friend I spoke to yesterday, plus three others; a skipper and four crew. They have fished every year for many years, in the case of this fellow for the last 12 years.
For example, in 1991, one of the two years that the minister is using as criteria for cancelling a licence, that crew caught about 150,000 to 180,000 pounds of fish over a 10-month period. Last year they caught roughly the same. In the two year period they caught just over
300,000	pounds of fish.
The fish plant manager or the collector buying the fish knows when the boat comes in, it has one great pile of fish in the hole. There are five men on board. Who owns which fish?
The convention that has grown up over the years is to sell the fish in the name of the skipper. It makes a lot of sense. Another way to do it I suppose if you follow the Crosbie dictum is to say: "Okay fellows. Count all the fish out, we want five equal piles here". That was not the way it was done. If that was the way he had wanted it done I suppose they would have done it that way. God knows fishermen have done sillier things at the direction of the government. They made the mistake of selling it all in one pile in the name of the skipper.
Now then the question. If DFO bureaucrats go out to find how much fish the other four fellows caught, they are going to find the answer real fast. Not one single pound. Not an ounce.
February 4, 1993

Now then let us go back to the minister's brave words of December 18. "If they did not catch any fish we are going to take their licence". What he really said is: "If you cannot prove you caught fish we are going to take your licence".
So you sit there and think that example cannot be real.
I will tell you how real it is. Just by coincidence this man called me three or four days ago and I just got back to calling him yesterday afternoon.
In the meantime, yesterday morning he had been visited by DFO. DFO went into the community and said to various people that some qualified for a licence and some did not. It said to one man standing beside my friend that DFO records showed he had caught six pounds last year and he qualified. Another man, my friend, was not on the list. He explained he was part of a crew that caught 150,000 pounds. That does not apply. He did not qualify for a licence.
It is now February 4. We are already one month into the year. DFO answers not to worry about it because he will be able to appeal it. He will and six weeks or two months down the road there is no doubt he will have his licence, come March, April or May.
Returning to my earlier comment about those who make obscene phone calls and those who trigger false fire alarms, this act is every bit as despicable because the sledge-hammer approach has inflicted unnecessary pain. This man I spoke to on the phone last night told me that if they took his fishing licence after 12 years, after fishing 10 months a year for 12 years, they might as well cut off both his arms. That is the kind of anguish that these cowardly, mean, costly policies of the government are inflicting.
So far, these are only my words on all of this. Let me give one other line of information.
I mentioned that these five people were fishing together and the fish were sold in the name of one person. All of that is true. Let me speak of something else that is true.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission over the years has actually figured a way to deal with this. It simply said the fishermen did not have to count their fish out in five piles. It was assumed if there were five people fishing together they each had one-fifth of the effort so the total value of the landing would be divided by five. Each one would be given credit for one-fifth of the
Government Orders
landing. On that basis the men would be paid unemployment insurance.
Over the years the men I am talking about have regularly fished for 10 months. On the basis of that fishing activity they have drawn UI for a couple of months. What better proof does one need?
What do we have here? One arm of the government, UIC, acknowledges not only that they have fished but that they have done such a good job they qualified for UI for a couple of months so they can get back in the boat. Another arm of the government, in this case fisheries, is saying because there is no record they have fished they will be deprived of their licence to fish and will be caused anguish. A sledge-hammer will be used on them.
Government is about collecting money. It is about spending money. But surely there has to be more reason to have a government than that.
Government is also about reflecting our values as a people. We are not a mean-spirited people. Government should not get its jollies out of making life miserable for fishermen or people who are seasonal workers, or people who are in the work place and have to make agonizing decisions because of harassment. Government ought not to be in the business of reflecting that kind of meanness of spirit. That is not the values we project as a society, that we hold as a people. Government ought to set the tone. This government is setting a tone but what an awful tone.
One of our values in society is that we have a work ethic. You would never know it by listening to the rhetoric of this government. This government has the idea that somehow there are 27 million lazy hangashores, as we call them in Newfoundland. A hangashore is a person who stays ashore because he is too lazy to go fishing.
The government has the idea that there are 27 million hangashores and it has to be the policeman guarding them. It has to make sure they get out of bed in the morning. It sets their alarm clocks for them, gets them out to work and hustles them off because they might all stay home and get beer bellies.
It might come as a shock to that crowd over there but some of those people, about 99 per cent of them, actually do want to work. I know people on welfare. I know people on unemployment insurance. I know people who are just scraping by. The litmus question to them at all times is: "Would you rather be doing what you are doing or working?" Every time the answer comes back: "I would rather have a job 12 months a year".

February 4, 1993
Government Orders
Until we get a government that believes in people, that reflects the values we hold as a society including the work ethic, until we can get rid of a government that gets its jollies out of putting people down, of denigrating people and suggesting that people are lazy hangashores, until we can achieve that it does not matter whether we give this crowd another whit of authority to borrow. They are going to spend like drunken sailors anyway.
All we can hope is that the time comes sooner rather than later that we put people on that side of the House who reflect rather than undermine the values of Canadian society.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on Bill C-98, the borrowing authority, by which the government seeks authority to borrow an additional $8.2 billion which is in addition to the budget that was laid down last fiscal year, the fiscal year we are still in, and the additional borrowing that took place last fall.
This will bring the government's borrowings above the budgeted amount by the $10 billion or $11 billion that the government goofed in its estimates in the last budget. This is not the first time that it has messed up in its estimates of the deficit. The deficit this year is now predicted to be $34.4 billion, $7 billion higher than what it said it would be at budget time.
This deficit is $10 billion higher than it should have been using the projections the government used in the budget before last. According to the estimates from two years ago the deficit that we now have is twice what it was projecting. The projections have been away off. Ever since 1988 the ministers of finance have been predicting lower and lower deficits and every year when the year comes to an end we discover that we are still in the low $30 billion range and we have not shaken out of that in all of those years.
Yet the Minister of Finance, the member for Etobicoke, who was the Minister of Finance for most of that period was unshaken. He said that he has the fundamentals right, he understands the economy and he has the solution. Yet every time he makes a prediction he is wrong. He has been so busy getting the fundamentals right that we now owe twice the national debt that we owed when he first became finance minister in this country. The debt that we are all paying as a result will now be in the neighbourhood of $40 billion worth of interest every year to sustain the debt that he has brought upon the people of Canada.
February 4, 1993

We have listened to some of the government members say that opposition members and backbenchers are wasting the time of the government by this discussion because really all we have before the House is a piddly little idea of borrowing more money and they should not get excited about that.
The fundamental reason that members of Parliament are in Parliament is to watch over and agree to the expenditures of government and the taxation that governments levy. If we are going to stand idly by and not say anything when governments come to us for further borrowings, we are falling down in our duty. The only way that that further borrowing can be paid is by future taxation and that is right within the ambit of every one of these backbenchers, whether they are on the government side or the opposition side. Our duty, the main reason we are sent here, is to overview and give approval or otherwise to the government's estimates for expenditure and its methods of creating that expenditure and paying for that expenditure through taxation.
This has been the reason for parliaments since before 1215 and the Magna Carta and it continues to be the basic right of parliamentarians. To imply that we are wasting time by discussing a mere borrowing bill misses the point precisely. I cannot understand why a government member would be so callous as to raise that as a legitimate argument.
This government has been sitting with its eyes closed to a great extent, if we listen to its view of what it has done for the economy. I in my riding and many others across the country who represent different regions saw
76,000	individuals and small businesses go bankrupt last year. It was a new record. We have never before had that proportion of bankruptcies, even at the height of the Great Depression in the 1930s.
It is only recently that the government has even been able to say the r word for recession, but the sad fact for most Canadians is that they have been in a depression for quite a long time. The government has been busy fighting inflation and through that it has to a great extent induced the recession and the depression.
We have been hearing about averages, and we all know the problems with averages. A wit once said that the economist and the statistician do not seem to understand the pain of an average. For instance, if a person had one foot in boiling water and another foot in freezing water they would say that on average the man should be comfortable. We know that is not the way comfort works.

We also know that using averages does not tell very much about the fight against inflation.
I represent a constituency in prairie Canada. I have watched the fight against inflation and I must say that it has been devastating. When I first came down here in 1980, farmland in my part of the country was considered to be worth about $800 or $900 an acre. Then governments began to discover inflation and decided that to fight inflation they would use extremely high interest rates, which they did. They put a lot of farmers out of business. They put a lot of villages out of business. They shut down a lot of farm suppliers. They depopulated parts of rural Canada. In the process they have managed to force the price of farmland and the value of all assets of the community from about $900 an acre down to less than $300 an acre.
The people I represent have paid a huge price in fighting inflation. The value of their assets has been cut by two-thirds at least. It does not matter whether they were home owners in one of the small towns or cities of my riding or farmers out in the country. If their assets were worth $1 million in 1980 and they have not increased the size of their business, farm or property, they are now worth $300,000. That is a tremendous contribution to inflation. In making that contribution they have less assets to borrow against and less assets to raise capital from.
The government has taken the view that everyone has to pay for inflation, and my friends and neighbours accept that. However they think they have paid a rather high price. They have paid an even higher price than just losing the value of their assets. They have paid a high price by losing their very incomes. For those who make their living on the farm there are numbers of ways of showing the losses in their farm incomes. I will use two methods that were put forward recently by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool.
The first method of discovering what losses farmers have put up with in the province of Saskatchewan alone would be to take the realized net farm income between 1980 and 1984 on average-and we use adjusted prices so that we do not have to worry about inflation; these are in 1992 dollars-and compare it with the realized net farm income for the years 1992 and the estimates for 1993. The shortfall would be in the neighbourhood of $880 million to $1.1 billion; a $880 million shortfall already realized for 1992 and the estimates for 1993 would indicate a $1.1 billion shortfall from the average realized net income of the early 1980s for Saskatchewan farmers.

We could use another test. We could take the average net farm income for farmers in the years 1980 and 1981 and compare them per worker against the realized average industrial wage per worker in Saskatchewan at the same time. We would find in 1980 and 1981 that those figures were almost the same. The farm worker received $13,500 and the industrial worker received $15,500. They were almost the same, just a few thousand dollars difference.
When we make that same comparison now after all the farm support that has gone into the farm community, we find that the average farm income in 1991 amounted to $6,700.74 per farm. How did the industrial worker make out in that same period? In 1991 his or her average industrial wage was $24,197. There was a vast change in that period of time.
I submit that part of the reason for that vast change was not only the trade war which occurred but also government policy which struck out all or most of the assets farm people had with which to refinance or to finance other ways of making farm income.
The fight against inflation and trying to get the so-called fundamentals right has really been harmful to rural people in my constituency and across the country.
I have discussed a little about the income shortfall as seen on a farm-by-farm basis and when compared to the average industrial wage in my province. If we look at the effect of the trade war on those incomes, we can extract some of the costs that have occurred because of the trade effects of that war as a result of various actions of both the European Community and the American government.
In 1985 the President of the United States introduced a farm bill which included the right of Americans to grant export enhancement funds to exporters. This had the effect of driving the competitive price of international grains down as much as $80 per tonne. Right now farmers in my community do not net $80 per tonne for most of their grain. We have an idea of how devastating this action by the Americans was and what it could do.
If we use the pre-trade war average price of grain in Saskatchewan alone and superimpose that trend, we see that because of the actions of the Americans and the response of the Europeans farm income in Saskatchewan shows a shortfall. Even with the government assistance that has been provided there is a shortfall of $6.7 billion from 1985 to the present. In those seven years we have had a $6.7 billion shortfall of income from the kind of income we normally are used to out there. It was almost $1 billion per year on average.
We have seen farm debt increase from $21 billion or $22 billion in 1986 or 1987 to in excess of $24 billion. I cite that because the Europeans and the Americans have not had the same kind of news to deal with. They are our two largest competitors. We are among the third largest exporters of grain and oilseeds, yet our farm incomes are falling behind the net farm incomes of those countries because frankly those countries care more about their farmers than do Canadian governments.
Using 1981 net total farm incomes as a base, European incomes fell over the decade of the 1980s by 16.5 per cent. American farm income over that same decade rose by 23 per cent at the same time as Canadian net farm incomes fell by 51.4 per cent.
We can see that farmers in the United States have been much better cared for by their governments than has been the case here. Their net incomes over the decade rose by 23 per cent, while ours fell by 51 per cent. This was done in the name of getting the fundamentals right and in the name of fighting inflation.
Government policy has continued to put pressure on farmers and their families. In the financial statement before Christmas the finance minister said there would be even further reductions to the government expenditures on grading and inspections in meat plants and in processing plants. That was accompanied later by announcements from some officials indicating that it was to be the intention of the Government of Canada to reduce grading and inspection standards to standards equivalent to those of the country to which we might be exporting.

In other words we would lower it to Mexican standards if we were thinking of selling to the Mexicans, or even lower if we were exporting to some country with standards lower than those of the Mexicans.
There was no explanation of how to separate product that had been so graded if it did not go to the particular country but instead ended up in the refrigerator of a consumer in Canada. There was no explanation of how we were to respond when some of our international customers said: "We used to buy your product because you had such high grading standards and we could always count on Canadian product meeting those standards".
Those good customers will start looking at our changed grading standards and say: "We might as well buy from the Americans who have a much looser arrangement than you have. We used to prefer your product because we could be sure that the standards would stand up and that we were buying quality. But if you are going to abandon that then I guess we will find another place to get our product". We will have to start looking for other customers.
This is a stupid way to become world competitive, all in the name of having the fundamentals right. I have spent some time showing how misguided some of the fundamentals were.
In that economic statement as well we heard the Minister of Finance say that the Crow benefit which western Canadians used to think was almost part of our constitutional heritage was to be degraded a bit more. We watched in the early 1980s as the Liberals backed away from their commitment to freight rates to an area that is land-locked and was developed on the basis of a secure transportation system. They backed out of that and have been presenting some money to the railways each year. At the moment it stands at about $730 million. The government has shown that it is no longer considering that a firm commitment. It has decided to back off bit by bit. It is taking 10 per cent away this year. That will mean about 8 cents to 10 cents a bushel less in the pockets of farmers next year, thanks to that little announcement.
It also sends a signal to farmers that the Crow rate is no longer anything that can be counted on. If a minister of the Crown who is in charge of finance can stand up and take 10 per cent of it away on a whim with an announcement in the House then there is nothing to stop him from taking 100 per cent of it away at some future date.
The residents of rural Canada are feeling less and less secure with this government. They see that this government does not have the fundamentals right. It cannot produce projections. It cannot guess right. It cannot do anything right. It is then time we made it veiy clear that the government should resign so we can have an election and find a replacement.

The House resumed from Ihesday, November 17, 1992, consideration of the motion of Mr. Whittaker:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of developing a healthy small business sector in Canada by targeting more federal contracts to the small business sector and establishing a more aggressive Buy Canada program.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak today in this debate on the motion of the hon. member for Okanagan-Si-milkameen-Merritt.
The motion reads as follows:
That the government should consider the advisability of developing a healthy small business sector in Canada by targeting more federal contracts to the small business sector and establishing a more aggressive Buy Canada program.
First, it must be said that the motion tabled by my hon. colleague is acceptable in principle. This government is always striving for a strong and diversified small business sector.
The government will always do its utmost for the thousands of hard-working business people who create

Private Members' Business
thousands of jobs that benefit all Canadians. Earlier in this debate, an outline of this government's many reforms concerning government procurement was given.
I must go back briefly to this outline so that we can clearly understand what the motion before us today means and, I might add, better realize the remarkable work done by the Minister of Supply and Services.
It is with the needs expressed by small businesses in mind that more than three years ago the Minister of Supply and Services decided to undertake a major reform of his department. Today, we are proud of our very fruitful co-operation with Canadian business people.
The new business practices of the department are based on five major objectives which I will briefly describe.
First is the use of a procurement system which is accessible and competitive. I am of course referring to the open invitation to bid, which allows any business person to tender for the contracts of his choice. Indeed, it is our small business people who select contracts based on their priorities and their potential, and do this using a personal computer.
The second objective has to do with the implementation of an impartial process to hear the complaints of suppliers, namely the Procurement Review Board, which is now part of the Canadian International Trade Tribunal. The board allows any contractor who feels he has been wronged to make representations. Some have successfully made their case.
Third, the support provided to the Canadian industry is confirmed by the new policy on Canadian content. Supply and Services Canada gives priority to procurement in Canada by limiting the competition to qualified Canadian suppliers of goods and services when there are enough of them to ensure competitiveness.
Fourth is a greater social and environmental responsibility. We are referring here to the employment equity, environmental protection and energy conservation requirements in dealing with suppliers.
Our fifth goal is to provide first-rate customer service, as is expected from a department like ours.
Our business partners are demanding and so are we of them. They understand our new approach and have expressed support for it.
In fact, this is the kind of offer that is hard to refuse: greater accessibility, improved efficiency, top-notch service and more chances of tendering for federal government contracts.
The competitive bidding system we have can be considered as a good tool for economic growth.
I am not saying that all suppliers should deal with the federal government. What I am saying is that those who choose to, for one reason or another, will be surprised to see how easy it is and will be able to improve their competitiveness.
As I read over my hon. colleague's motion, I must point out a minor aberration which shows the weakness of the motion being debated as it relates to public procurement.
My hon. colleague would like the small business sector to get more contracts. Fine, but let him know first that 80 per cent of our suppliers are small and medium-sized businesses at this time. That is right, 80 per cent. If you factor in contracting-out, it would be closer to 90 per cent. This goes to show that small and medium-sized businesses are truly major players in the area of federal government contracts.
I could emphasize other highly positive aspects of our reforms which are intended to be forward looking. The main thing is that Canadian entrepreneurs wanted a chance to compete and the government responded swiftly to this perfectly legitimate request.
This debate is an opportunity for me to reaffirm that this government is making every effort to assist our small and medium-sized businesses in looking for new markets, to promote their competitiveness by giving them more opportunities to compete for federal government contracts and to assert themselves on the international markets.
Therefore, the motion put forward by the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt runs counter to measures that have been in place for over two years. Worse, it suggests that our small and medium-sized businesses lack vitality, that our entrepreneurs lack initiative and that risk is never rewarded. It also suggests that government ignores the demands of the Canadian small-business sector, when nothing is further from the truth.
This attitude does not surprise me but I must say that it does not at all suit the economic challenges facing this country. By the way, I want to assure the hon. member that any suggestion of his will receive due consideration, provided that it can foster the financial security of our fellow citizens.

Supply and Services' initiatives have been given a warm welcome throughout the country, and I can tell you that civil servants themselves are happy to work in a setting considerably more stimulating, although more demanding.
Day after day, we are happy to demonstrate that the Government of Canada can innovate and be efficient. This is great news for the taxpayers as well as for us who administer their tax money. The future depends on it.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise today to speak to this bill that has been brought to this House by the member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt, a seat-mate of mine in the Chamber. He is the NDP critic for the small business sector.
The member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt has been a very strong spokesperson for the small business sector in this House and to the government on quite a number of matters. The issue in this motion today is just one of the many that he has been able to raise. I am very glad to be able to speak both in support of this motion and in support of the small business sector that is being promoted in the member's motion.
The member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt in presenting this motion to the House had a couple of very astute things to say, and I just wanted to briefly quote him before I enter into my own remarks. The member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt said: "This government has given lip-service to improving the business climate in Canada and this would be an ideal time for it to show some positive action for the small business sector through its support of a buy Canada, buy small business program".
The member also said: "It is only by opening the bidding process and guaranteeing that contracts are awarded to small Canadian businesses through a buy Canadian, buy small business program that we will ensure small businesses continue to create jobs in the economy and help bring us out of our continuing recession".
Those are very important words for us and for the government to hear today as it is contemplating the

various actions that can be taken to assist the small business sector in the work that it is doing.
I would also like to indicate to this House how important this matter is. I know, Mr. Speaker, that you are a very strong supporter of the small business sector and are aware of its importance to the Canadian economy. More than 97 per cent of businesses in Canada are small businesses with fewer than 50 employees.
In 1989 small businesses maintained a labour force of more than 3.75 million people, equivalent to over one-third of the total private sector employment in all of Canada. From 1981 to 1989 small businesses created 81.5 per cent of new jobs in Canada. At the same time this has been a very difficult time for small businesses.
Just yesterday the newest bankruptcy figures were released. In 1992 there were 14,317 business bankruptcies in Canada. That is an increase of 821 over the 13,496 businesses who declared bankruptcy in 1991.
The recession is very hard on the small business sector, which is a large employer and a major stabilizing factor in many of our small communities and major cities.
The Government of Canada can play a very important role in the development of programs that would be of some assistance to small businesses, and that goes beyond tax measures and other matters. We all know there are negative and positive tax measures that can be utilized to assist businesses.
The most negative tax measure has been the implementation of the goods and services tax that small business people right across the country have said has harmed them significantly. That is something that could be eliminated as soon as possible. It would certainly be eliminated if the New Democratic Party were elected after the next federal election.
There is another side to all of this too, and that is what the member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt is getting at in the motion before us today. The Department of Supply and Services purchases about $8 billion in goods and services every year for the Government of Canada; 60 per cent on a competitive basis and 40 per cent on a non-competitive basis. This is a very important and significant component of the way in which government money, which is being spent anyway, can be targeted toward small businesses in Canada.

The buy Canadian program suggested by my colleague is a very important way for the government to adapt some of its current policies to assist the small business sector. Earmarking just a portion of this supply and services' contracted money specifically for Canadian businesses would be of great assistance, particularly to those businesses that operate in rural and remote areas.
I want to give a couple of examples from my own constituency about how significant this might be. Economic development in rural constituencies is a difficult task at the best of times. Sometimes the stabilizing force of a contract is all that is needed to get a rural business, particularly a manufacturing or a processing business, under way. A lot of activity is taking place on the drawing board in northwest Saskatchewan that could utilize some of this sort of kick-starting that is available from government policy and program development.
The Western Diversification Office has indicated that a program it would be able to fit in is one to assist with the production of ethanol from grain stocks on the prairies. The government should make a very strong commitment to ensuring that ethanol product is available for purchase by producers. It is the same thing with the production of energy. Governments can play a very important role in ensuring that the energy produced from co-generation facilities by independent producers in rural and northern isolated communities is purchased by the utilities.
More important is the whole area of aboriginal economic development. The government has paid a lot of lip-service to this area and in fact has put some programming in place to ensure that aboriginal communities can be involved in generating revenues which would be useful in helping the people who live in the aboriginal communities.
The most negative aspect about economic development in aboriginal communities is that the money can be put in place for capital but it is not in place for operations. You can buy equipment and set up a manufacturing or processing operation but the problem comes in being able to maintain that operation while the business person in the aboriginal community is out searching for markets, et cetera.
If this government established a set-aside program under a buy Canadian umbrella for aboriginal economic development, ensuring that 10 per cent of certain budgets, for example the national defence budget, was being used to purchase products from these aboriginal manufacturing plants, it would have a stabilizing effect on that aboriginal community and that aboriginal business. It would certainly ensure that all of the activities engaged in at that manufacturing plant would be enhanced and allowed to grow. We would have a guaranteed contract in place to produce the duffle bags for the armed forces or whatever the purchase might be. They would have the ability to finance operations while they are looking for the other contracts that would expand and ensure the success of those aboriginal businesses. To me that is a very important matter.
We have to make sure the rural business infrastructure is maintained. We have to ensure that we do have the ability to purchase at the local level.
Most members of Parliament in this Chamber will realize that we have very little ability to utilize our budgets for purchasing locally. Most of our stationery, as you are aware, Mr. Speaker, is purchased centrally in the House of Commons. It would be nice to be able to support local businesses through local purchasing.
I am quite concerned about the free trade agreement and the North American free trade agreement and how they affect the ability of the Government of Canada to enter into a buy Canadian program. The free trade agreement with the United States currently hinders the ability of Canada to have a buy Canadian program, a Canadian sourcing program of some kind, a Canadian government policy, a Canadian value-added profit policy, et cetera, because the free trade agreement prevents purchases over $29,000 from being set under those guidelines.
One of the very first things that this government has to do is cancel the free trade agreement so that we can have in place a complete buy Canadian program. It is even more important because we are about to enter into a new agreement with Mexico and the United States, the North American free trade agreement.
February 4, 1993

Mr. Speaker, this issue of small and medium-sized businesses is frequently discussed here in the House of Commons, as it was in Quebec's National Assembly when I had the privilege to serve there as MNA. As years went by, unfortunately, alot was said but very little was done for small and medium-sized businesses across the country. The facts show that small and medium-sized businesses create more jobs than all corporations put together. In fact, the number of jobs is even three to four times higher. But when we look at industrial subsidies in the country, we realize it is easy for big businesses to get all sorts of benefits from the government. However, the government keeps saying that it is encouraging small and medium-sized business which is creating jobs.
I would like to draw to your attention the fact that in the past organizations were established to defend small and medium-sized businesses. There was one in particular which I remember. It was called Business Warriors and was based in Toronto. I recall that they had the opportunity to defend their opinion that small businesses received comparatively less tax benefits or grants than large corporations. And they made their point with supporting evidence that small and medium-sized businesses were indeed penalized.
So, the case before us is still the same. How can we help small and medium-sized businesses? And the motion presented by one of the opposition parties brings back to the surface the kind of program we could set up in order to really help small and medium-sized businesses develop themselves and compete.
Competitiveness is the in word today. If companies, no matter how big, cannot expand, we cannot expect them to make great progress in being competitive. The suggestions I would like to make, after listening to numerous debates on this matter concerning small businesses, is
Private Members' Business
that we should focus on programs in a concrete way and not on bills or regulations 200 or 300 pages long. The first thing we should do is visit small businesses. Some associations and individuals that are very articulate could tell us about the needs of small businesses, about the tools they need to expand and be really competitive. That is what they are asking for.
Just because they make those suggestions does not mean they will get carte blanche for everything they need. There is always some leeway. They know that. They can tell, with the evidence to prove it, what they need in order to expand. But if they do not have a chance to speak out on these things, we will never be able to find out what would help small businesses to grow.
Some of them have been very successful in this country. Over the Christmas holidays, I read Mr. Bombardier's story. It is amazing to think that he two of his brothers began the business in his garage. That gives you an idea of how important all that can be. I also read that many inventions do not come from laboratories at a cost of millions of dollars. In the past 50 years, most big discoveries, like Xerox, for example, were made by people working in their own basement or in a garage.
Entrepreneurship exists, but one must be watching out for it. I am convinced that if those people could say what they need, we on our side with the resources, experience and statistics available could easily show that there is some room to manoeuvre and we could write up in a few pages what is needed for them to develop.
That is extremely important, not only for confidence or competitiveness but also for encouraging other people. They would feel supported. You know that confidence is extremely important in international affairs or in other things.
I would like to give you an example of this. One of our colleagues here from the Liberal Party, the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, did a terrific job on the possibility of using grain to make ethanol and derivatives. Research has been done on this and it has been shown that this industry, which is now very small, given the required resources could become a major industry in our country, not only for the environment but also for the tremendous spin-off benefits.

February 4, 1993
Private Members' Business
However, if they do not have government resources to help them start up, we cannot expect miracles. Times are pretty tough, so that is all the more reason to give them moral support, financial support, of course, and technical support. Luckily, we have the National Research Council which has an international reputation and can help them.
We could talk about it for a long time and we know that there have been many discussions and debates on small and medium-sized businesses. First, because they belong to associations, they must speak out on the issue because they are out in the field, they know the needs. We can be guided by what they can do, what they know and especially what they want in setting up a real program. With that, I am convinced that the "Buy Canada" program mentioned in the motion could follow automatically, because if we enter a new field where no one has been before, we will certainly be the best and over time we will be very competitive. So we would buy Canadian not just out of pride but because it was a rapidly growing field and we would have the necessary skills and entrepreneurship.
Many ideas could be submitted. A famous saying of Einstein comes to mind: Imagination is more important than intelligence. Of course, we take it for granted that a certain amount of intelligence is required and I am sure it exists, but imagination is the key to advancement. Small and medium-sized business is the most important engine of our country's development. We are a nation of 27 million and we have shown that we can play an extremely important role on the world stage with our inventions and developments and so on. We have proven ourselves.
I could give examples of technologies, like fibre optics, where we were world leaders. However, that technology has been sold and today it is the Japanese who are developing it secretly. But that is another matter.
In conclusion, are should call on those who are in the field. We have public moneys to supplement what they do not have at their disposal in terms of research and funding. That program will be the real beginning. It will be the basis. I am convinced that it is the only answer, and the most needed one.
